components.description: Show one section at a time, or several, and keep long pages scannable.

keyboard: Tab: move between the headers
Enter / Space: open or close the focused panel
aria: Each trigger is a button with aria-expanded and aria-controls; each panel is labelled by its trigger
a11y.notes: hiddenUntilFound lets the browser's page search find and open closed panels.

parts.name: Accordion
parts.description: Tracks which items are open: one at a time by default, several if you allow it. You pick a look (plain, divided, contained, separated) and a density.

parts.name: AccordionItem
parts.description: One section of the list. It draws the divider, the card or the hover fill, depending on the look of the list.

parts.name: AccordionTrigger
parts.description: The header row: a real button inside a heading. It can hold a leading icon, a second line, a slot for extra info and an indicator.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The question or section name inside the trigger. It is also the button's accessible name.

parts.name: Meta
parts.description: A slot between the label and the indicator, for a counter, a status or a short value.

parts.name: Indicator
parts.description: The chevron or plus that shows whether the item is open. Its style and position follow the look of the list unless you set them.

parts.name: AccordionContent
parts.description: The panel under the trigger. It opens smoothly to the height of its content, and its text lines up with the label.

parts.name: AccordionRow
parts.description: Wraps the trigger so a control can sit beside it, not inside it: a checkbox or switch on the left, or an action button such as Edit.

parts.name: AccordionFeedback
parts.description: The loading, empty and error content of a panel, with an optional action such as Retry.

items.text: Pick one look per list: divided or plain on a page, contained as one card, separated for stand-alone sections.
Use the compact density (36 px rows) in side panels and the default (48 px rows) everywhere else.
Allow several open items when people compare answers. By default, opening one closes the other.
Write the trigger as the question or section name in sentence case, like How do refunds work? It is the button's accessible name.
Put controls beside the trigger with AccordionRow. The trigger stays a single button and the control gets its own Tab stop.
Don't put buttons or links inside the trigger. The whole row is already a button, and a button inside a button is invalid HTML.
Don't hide what people must read or do in a closed row. Required information and primary actions belong outside the accordion.

props.name: capacity

parts.name: Avatar
parts.description: The round or square frame in five sizes. Set a colour for tinted initials or the primary variant for a filled one; interactive makes it a button, selected adds a check badge and disabled dims it.

parts.name: AvatarImage
parts.description: The photo, an img with src and alt. It shows once loaded; until then, or when the URL fails, the fallback stays in place.

parts.name: AvatarFallback
parts.description: Initials or an icon, shown while the image loads or when there is none. The text size follows the avatar size.

parts.name: AvatarBadge
parts.description: A dot on the top right corner, centred on the circle's edge or the square's corner. A status sets a presence dot with a shape per status and an accessible name that defaults to the status.

parts.name: AvatarLabel
parts.description: An avatar with a name and a second line, and optionally a capacity bar or a control at the end. It is a plain div. It replaces PersonCell and UserInfo, which still render the same row.

items.text: Use an Avatar to show who a person or workspace is, next to their name. For several people in little space, use Avatar Group.
Always add a fallback with initials, also when there is an image. It covers the moment before the photo loads and a broken image URL.
Use a circle for a person and a square for an entity such as a workspace, team or project, so the shape already tells which one it is.
Keep one colour per person. The tints are theme tokens, so initials stay readable in dark mode.
Show presence with the badge and say it in text where it matters, such as Away next to the name. Each status has its own shape, so colour is never the only signal.
Give an interactive avatar an accessible name with aria-label, for example Account menu, Nora Lindgren. Its initials are not a name.
Don't resize an avatar with your own size classes. Pick one of the sizes: initials, icon and presence dot scale with it.
Don't use colour to carry status or meaning. Tone is an identity colour; status needs the presence dot, a word, or both.
Don't combine selected with a presence dot. The check badge and the dot sit on the same corner, so one hides the other.
Next to a single 20 px line of text use size="3xs", so the avatar is as tall as the text.

components.title: Avatar Group
components.description: A stack of overlapping avatars, with an optional overflow count.

props.name: max
props.description: With `people`: how many faces show before the count. Default 3.

props.name: people
props.description: A list of people: the group renders their avatars itself, overlapping by 4 px (2 px at `sm` and `xs`, so the second initial is not hidden under the next face), cut at `max` with a "+N" avatar. Hovering a face lifts it and shows the name in…

props.name: size
props.description: With `people`: the avatar size, `sm` 24 px, `xs` 28 px, `default` 36 px, `lg` 40 px, `xl` 44 px. Default `sm`.

parts.name: AvatarGroup
parts.description: The row. It overlaps its avatars with a ring in the surface colour, or spaces them with a 6 px gap; hovering one lifts it and nudges its neighbours, except with reduced motion.

parts.name: Avatar
parts.description: Each person: an Avatar with initials or an image. Give all avatars in one group the same size.

parts.name: AvatarGroupCount
parts.description: The +N circle at the end for everyone not shown, as a static count or a button. It takes the size of the avatars.

items.text: Use an Avatar Group to show who is on a project or document, composing each avatar yourself. For people passed as data with a built-in limit, pass people, max and size instead of children (a people list lifts on hover and names each face in a Tooltip too).
Cut the list yourself and put the rest in the count as +3. The group renders every child it gets; it does not count or hide anyone.
Make the count a button when people can open the rest. Give it an aria-label such as Show 3 more people and aria-expanded.
Place the group on a surface that sets the surface colour, such as a Card. The rings take that colour, so each avatar reads as cut out of the background.
Pick overlap for a header or a row where room is short, and spaced for a short list where each face should stay whole.
Don't mix avatar sizes in one group. The overlap and the count circle assume one size for every avatar.
Don't use a group for a single person, or for a list people should read name by name. Use Avatar, or AvatarLabel with a name.
At sm and xs the faces overlap by 2 px so both initials stay readable; do not tighten them further with your own spacing.

components.title: Badge
components.description: A small status or category label in 12 colors and 6 styles.

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

parts.name: Badge
parts.description: A short label in a rounded box, in 12 colors, 6 styles, two sizes (20 or 24 px) and a rounded or pill shape. As a button or link it gains hover, focus and press states.

parts.name: Leading mark
parts.description: A Lucide icon as a child, or a dot. The icon is 12 px on a small badge and 14 px on a medium one, follows the label color, and sits 4 or 6 px before it.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: One short line, 12 px semibold on a small badge and 14 px on a medium one. It never wraps and clips what does not fit, so keep the label to a word or two.

parts.name: Remove button
parts.description: A 16 px round button with an X, drawn when a remove handler is set. It is a separate button with its own name and the badge itself stays inert; it is left out when the badge is a button or link.

parts.name: BadgeCell
parts.description: A Badge for a table cell, made from a label string, with the light border style by default.

parts.name: BadgeCounter
parts.description: A count next to a label, or on the corner of an icon button, in neutral, brand or danger tones. Counts above 99 read 99+, and an overlay counter hides itself at zero.

parts.name: BadgeIndicator
parts.description: A small signal: unread, presence (online, away, busy, offline) or a symbol (check, warning, lock). Each kind has its own shape, not only its own color, and carries an accessible name.

parts.name: BadgeProcessing
parts.description: A running operation and its result: pending (a turning spinner), success or error. The label always names the state.

parts.name: Chip
parts.description: An interactive pill that filters, selects or opens a list. Selection shows as the indigo tint and a mark, never as color alone.

parts.name: EntityChip
parts.description: A person, team or workspace as a pill: a 24 px mark (an avatar, an image, a flag) before the name, and an optional remove button. Written `<Chip variant="entity">`; EntityChip is a deprecated alias.

parts.name: TokenChip
parts.description: One entry inside a multi-value field, such as an email address. An invalid token gets a warning icon and the red tint; the field names the error. Written `<Chip variant="token">`; TokenChip is a deprecated alias.

items.text: Use a Badge for a short status or category on a row, card or heading: Paid, Draft, Beta. For the change in a number use Trend Chip, and for a message people have to read use Alert.
Give each status one color and keep it wherever that status appears. Write the status in the label as well, so color is never the only cue.
Use the light or light border style in tables and lists, and keep the solid style for the one badge that should stand out.
Render the badge as a button when it does something. Only a button or link gets the pointer cursor, the hover ring and the focus ring.
Put an overlay counter on the corner of a relatively positioned button and name the count in the button, like Notifications, 3 unread. The counter itself stays decorative.
Use Chip for a filter or a choice. It announces its selected state and shows a mark as well as the tint.
Don't use a Badge as a selection control. A removable tag takes a remove handler; anything that selects or opens a list is a Chip.
Don't recolor a badge with classes or hex values. Every color and style pair is measured for AA contrast in light and dark mode.
Don't put two badges on one heading, or a badge on every row of a list. A badge that is everywhere says nothing.

components.title: Breadcrumb
components.description: Shows the user's location in a hierarchy, in the `plain`, `contained` or `underline` look.

keyboard: Tab between the links
aria: nav with aria-label "breadcrumb"; the current page has aria-current="page"; separators are hidden from screen readers

parts.name: Breadcrumb
parts.description: The nav landmark named breadcrumb. Variant sets the look (plain, contained or underline), and density (36 px or 28 px rows) switches to the sized layout on one line.

parts.name: BreadcrumbList
parts.description: The ordered list of items and separators. Contained draws the border and surface and underline the line below; without density it wraps to a second line when room runs out.

parts.name: BreadcrumbItem
parts.description: One step of the trail, a list item holding a link or, at the end, the current page.

parts.name: BreadcrumbLink
parts.description: A level above the current page, a link that can hold an icon before the text. Truncated limits it to 160 px with an ellipsis and the full name as its title.

parts.name: BreadcrumbSeparator
parts.description: A list item between two items, hidden from screen readers. It shows a chevron, a slash, or your own icon.

parts.name: BreadcrumbEllipsis
parts.description: A button that stands for hidden middle levels. Use it as the trigger of a Popover that lists them; it shows an open state.

parts.name: BreadcrumbPage
parts.description: The current page as text, not a link, marked as the current page. It can be truncated like a link.

parts.name: BreadcrumbSiblingTrigger
parts.description: A separate button beside a link that opens a list of sibling pages. The link still navigates; the chevron turns when the list is open.

parts.name: BreadcrumbRestricted
parts.description: A level the person cannot open. It stays in the trail with a lock, is focusable and explains itself through its title.

parts.name: BreadcrumbLoading
parts.description: A quiet placeholder for the current level while its name loads. It is a status region; there is no spinner.

items.text: Use a Breadcrumb on nested pages, such as one project's settings, so people see where they are and can step back up. For switching between sibling views, use Tabs.
End the trail with BreadcrumbPage, not a link. It is marked as the current page, so screen readers announce where the person is.
Put a separator between items yourself; the list does not add them. Each one sits in its own list item and is hidden from assistive technology.
Pass a density to get the sized layout: 36 px rows with hover underline, pressed fill and focus ring. Without it the trail is the small inline list.
Collapse deep trails to the root, the parent and the current page. Put the hidden levels behind an ellipsis that opens a list of links, in their real order.
Keep a restricted level visible with BreadcrumbRestricted instead of removing it, so the trail stays truthful.
Show the trail as one link to the parent page below 360 px of width.
Don't link the current page or mark a link as current by hand. BreadcrumbPage already marks the last step and is not clickable.
Don't show a spinner while the current name loads. Use BreadcrumbLoading, a quiet placeholder with the right accessible name.
Don't use a breadcrumb as the only way to move around. It shows the path to the page, not every page there is.

components.title: Button
components.description: The main action trigger, in 11 variants, 2 shapes and 5 sizes.

props.name: className
props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: focusableWhenDisabled
props.description: Whether the button should be focusable when disabled.

props.name: nativeButton
props.description: Whether the component renders a native `<button>` element when replacing it via the `render` prop. Set to `false` if the rendered element is not a button (for example, `<div>`).

props.name: pending
props.description: Shows a spinner in place of the leading icon and ignores presses. The button stays focusable and keeps its colour (it is not disabled).

props.name: phase
props.description: Async feedback: pending shows a spinner, success a check, error a retry icon. The label is yours (for example Saving…, Saved, Retry). Keep the width constant with a fixed width on the button so it does not jump between phases.

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

props.name: style
props.description: Style applied to the element, or a function that returns a style object based on the component's state.

keyboard: Enter / Space: activate
aria: Renders a native <button>; with `render` set to another element pass nativeButton={false} so the button role and keys are kept
a11y.notes: Disabled buttons leave the tab order unless focusableWhenDisabled is set.

parts.name: Button
parts.description: A native button that fits its content. Variant sets the look, size the height (32 to 48 px), shape rounded or pill, and pending shows a spinner and ignores presses.

parts.name: Leading icon
parts.description: An icon before the label, with 2 px less padding on that side. It is 16 px at small and medium, up to 24 px at the largest sizes, and a spinner replaces it while pending.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The text, 14 px medium (16 px at xl, 18 px at 2xl). Write a verb and its object, such as Save changes, and keep it on one line.

parts.name: Trailing icon
parts.description: An icon after the label, for a direction such as an arrow or a chevron.

parts.name: ButtonCell
parts.description: A small plain button for a secondary action in a table row.

items.text: Use a Button for an action on the current page, such as save, send or open a dialog. To go to another page, render the button as a link.
Give each view one primary or gradient button for its main action. Other actions are plain or links, and icon-only controls in a row, toolbar, field or card are ghost IconButtons.
Label a button with a verb and its object, like Save changes or Invite member. A destructive button repeats its action, and the one beside it says Cancel.
Show an async result on the button itself: Save changes, Saving, Saved, Retry. Give it a fixed width so it does not jump, and explain an error in a message nearby.
Give an icon-only control an aria-label and build it with IconButton, not a Button with an icon and no label.
Don't use outline for ordinary secondary actions. Those are plain; outline is an indigo-rimmed accent for the rare case that needs one.
Don't set heights or padding by hand. Pick a size, so compact and comfortable density both stay right.
Don't make destructive the default button. Name the action, like Delete workspace, and put a plain Cancel next to it.
Don't disable a button without saying why. Explain it in a message or tooltip, or keep the button enabled and explain the error after the press.

props.description: Style applied to the element, or a function that returns a style object based on the component's state.

keyboard: Enter / Space: activate
aria: Icon only: give it aria-label — a tooltip is not a name

parts.name: IconButton
parts.description: A native button with one icon in a square or circle, named by aria-label since it has no text. Pending and phase show async feedback in the same square; expanded marks an open trigger.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: The child: a Lucide icon with a 1.5 stroke, sized 16, 18, 20, 22 or 24 px by button size, in the text colour. The whole square is the hit area.

parts.name: IconButtonTextCell
parts.description: A table cell with a small plain icon button beside a label. The label becomes the button's name and falls back to Action.

items.text: Use an IconButton for a frequent action with an unmistakable icon: close, edit, more options. When the icon alone could be misread, use a Button with a text label.
Give every IconButton an aria-label that names the action: Delete invoice, not Trash. A tooltip is extra help, not the name.
Use plain for a secondary icon action with its own box and ghost for an icon-only control inside a row, toolbar, field or card. The default is primary, and a view has one primary action.
Pass a label to IconButtonTextCell. Without it every row's button is announced as Action.
Show a running action with pending or phase instead of swapping the icon yourself. Change the aria-label with the phase: Copy link, Copying link, Link copied.
Put the badge count in the name: Notifications, 3 unread. Draw the counter on a relative wrapper and hide it from assistive technology; the badge is not a second button.
Use expanded on a trigger that opens a menu or panel, and a Toggle with one stable name for a state that stays on, such as Favorite. Pressed (the click) and selected look different.
Don't use the small sizes as the only control on a touch screen. Pick the two largest, which reach the 44 px hit area touch needs.

components.title: Button Group
components.description: A row of connected buttons sharing borders and outer corners, for view switchers or segmented actions.

props.name: orientation
props.description: "horizontal" puts the buttons in a row, "vertical" stacks them with shared edges.

props.name: children
props.description: The label of the action part.

props.name: className
props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Disables both parts.

props.name: focusableWhenDisabled
props.description: Whether the button should be focusable when disabled.

props.name: groupClassName
props.description: Class names for the group wrapping both parts.

props.name: icon
props.description: Leading icon of the action part. Decorative.

props.name: menu
props.description: The entries of the menu: DropdownMenuItem, DropdownMenuSeparator and so on.

props.name: menuLabel
props.description: Accessible name of the menu part. Default "More actions".

props.name: menuProps
props.description: Props for the menu popup, for example `align`. Default `align="end"`.

props.name: nativeButton
props.description: Whether the component renders a native `<button>` element when replacing it via the `render` prop. Set to `false` if the rendered element is not a button (for example, `<div>`).

props.name: onAction
props.description: Runs when the action part is pressed.

props.name: open
props.description: Controlled open state of the menu.

props.name: pending
props.description: Shows a spinner in place of the leading icon and ignores presses. The button stays focusable and keeps its colour (it is not disabled).

props.name: phase
props.description: Async feedback: pending shows a spinner, success a check, error a retry icon. The label is yours (for example Saving…, Saved, Retry). Keep the width constant with a fixed width on the button so it does not jump between phases.

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

props.name: size
props.description: Same sizes as the Button. The Figma "Medium 40" is `size="lg"`; the default stays the Button default `md`.

props.name: style
props.description: Style applied to the element, or a function that returns a style object based on the component's state.

props.name: variant
props.description: "plain" (default) is a white button with a border, "solid" the primary fill.

parts.name: ButtonGroup
parts.description: A row, or a stack when vertical, that joins its children so only the two outer ends keep their corners. Shape is rounded or pill, and you name the group with an aria-label.

parts.name: Button
parts.description: Each direct child, usually a plain Button or Icon Button of the same size. The group sets the corners and overlaps borders, and the focused button moves on top so its ring shows.

parts.name: Shared edge
parts.description: One border between two neighbours: the next button overlaps the border of the previous one by 1 px, so two buttons never draw a double line.

parts.name: SplitButton
parts.description: Two parts: the action with its label and optional icon, and a chevron that opens a Dropdown Menu. Each has its own hover, pressed and open fill; keyboard focus shows through the fill, with no ring.

items.text: Use a Button Group for a few related actions that belong together, such as share, export and print, or zoom in and zoom out. For one choice that stays selected, use a Segment or a Radio Button Group.
Give the group an aria-label that names what the buttons do together, such as Zoom. It is already a group, but has no name.
Use the same variant and size on every button, and plain buttons in most cases. Shared borders only line up when the buttons have the same height and border.
Name every icon-only button in a group with an aria-label, and keep to one kind of content: all text, all icons, or all icon and text.
Use a Split Button when one action is far more common than its alternatives, and put the alternatives in its menu.
Don't wrap the buttons in extra elements. Only direct children get the joined corners, so a wrapper breaks the edges.
Don't put a primary or gradient button in the group. Joined buttons read as equals, and a view has one main action.
Don't use a group to pick an option. Joined buttons look like a choice but have no selected state, so use a Segment.

components.title: Card
components.description: A bordered container for grouping related content.

parts.name: Card
parts.description: The surface, in a default, elevated or outlined style, with 16 px padding and gaps (12 px when small) and a 16 px corner radius. It can be horizontal, interactive or selected.

parts.name: CardMedia
parts.description: An image area flush with the top edge, or the left edge in a horizontal card. Put an image inside to fill it; empty, it shows a placeholder, and a ratio replaces the fixed 160 px height.

parts.name: CardHeader
parts.description: A grid for the title, the description and an optional action on the right, with an icon tile or avatar at the left if you want one.

parts.name: CardTitle
parts.description: The title of the card. It renders a div, so put a heading inside it when the card opens a section of the page.

parts.name: CardDescription
parts.description: Secondary text under the title, in the secondary text colour.

parts.name: CardAction
parts.description: Sits top right in the header, for a menu button or one small button. It stays there however long the title runs.

parts.name: CardContent
parts.description: The body of the card. Anything goes in it: text, a list, a form, a chart.

parts.name: CardFooter
parts.description: A row of buttons with a line above it, aligned right, split with a note, equal width or stacked. The line can be removed, and the card drops its bottom padding when a footer is present.

parts.name: CardBody
parts.description: The text column of a horizontal card, next to the media. It carries the vertical padding the card does not have itself.

parts.name: CardIcon
parts.description: An icon tile for the header's leading slot: a tint surface and the icon in the tint text colour.

parts.name: CardMeta
parts.description: A row for a date, a status, a category or people, in small secondary text. It wraps on a narrow card.

parts.name: CardIndicator
parts.description: The radio or checkbox mark at the top right of a selectable card. It is decorative, since the card or its trigger carries the role and checked state.

parts.name: CardTrigger
parts.description: A button that covers the whole card, for a card that also holds other controls. It is the card's only focus stop, and the other controls sit above it.

parts.name: CardFeedback
parts.description: The data states of the whole card: loading (a skeleton), empty, error and denied, each with an optional title, description and action.

parts.name: CardBanner
parts.description: A strip at the top of a card: refreshing while the data stays visible, or an error with Retry when the last data stays visible.

parts.name: CardDragHandle
parts.description: The grip for cards in a sortable list such as a board. Every drag needs a keyboard alternative, such as a Move to menu.

items.text: Use a Card to group the content of one thing, like a project, a plan or a settings section. For a row use Item Card, for one number Metric Card, for nothing to show yet Empty State.
Leave the padding to the card. It matches the chart, stat and metric cards, and the small size suits dense grids, so don't override padding classes.
Put a menu button or one small button in the card action. It stays top right however long the title runs.
To make the whole card the target, set it interactive and give it a role (link, button or radio) and an aria-label.
When a card holds other controls, use a CardTrigger as the one target and raise the other controls above it.
Use plain buttons in a card footer when cards repeat in a grid. A view has one main action, and a gradient button on every card leaves none.
Show data states on the card: CardFeedback for loading, empty, error and no access, CardBanner when old data stays visible while it refreshes or after a failed refresh.
Pick the footer layout by content: end for a normal row of actions, between when a note sits beside them, stretch or stacked for a narrow card.
Don't put a button inside a card that is itself a button or a link. Use a CardTrigger, or keep the card static.
Don't set a white or hex background on a card. The card colour follows the theme and dark mode, and the parts inside read it.

keyboard: Space: check or uncheck
aria: role=checkbox with aria-checked ("mixed" when indeterminate)
Needs a label: wrap it in Label or use Field

parts.name: Checkbox
parts.description: The box: a 16 px square with a 4 px radius. Checked or indeterminate it is filled with the brand colour, and its hit area reaches 12 px sideways and 8 px up and down.

parts.name: Check indicator
parts.description: The check, or a dash while indeterminate. Its stroke is drawn in when the box is ticked, and Checkbox renders it for you.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The text that names the box. With a label the whole row is the click target, and without one the box needs an aria-label.

parts.name: Error message
parts.description: A line under the row in 12 px error colour, indented to the text. It sits outside the label, so it is not part of the box's name, and it marks the box invalid and is linked with aria-describedby.

items.text: Use a Checkbox for an on or off choice in a form, or to pick several items from a list. For a setting that takes effect at once use Switch, and for one choice out of several use Radio Group.
Give every checkbox a visible label. It is joined to the box, so a click on the text toggles it and a screen reader announces the label with the value.
Write the label as the choice itself, like Email me about new releases. Put a sentence of detail in the description under it.
Use indeterminate on a select-all box while only some rows are chosen. Work it out from the rows and state its scope, like Select all acts on the 5 members shown.
State the rule of a group above it, and put the error under the group, not on one row, like Choose at least two topics.
Show the error on a required box only after the first try to continue, and say what to do, like Accept the terms to create your account.
Don't import CheckboxField in new code. It is a deprecated alias of Checkbox, so use Checkbox with the same props.
Don't build a checkbox from a styled div. The component already handles Space, the focus ring and the larger hit area around the small box.
Don't use a checkbox for a setting that applies at once. A box looks like part of a form that is saved later, so use a Switch.
Don't offer indeterminate as a choice. It only displays a partial selection, and people can never pick it.
Don't show the error before the first try. A red box on load reads as a mistake the person has not made yet.

components.description: A toggle control for a binary setting.

props.name: appearance
props.description: Checked-track colour: `brand`, `neutral` (inverse black/white) or `muted` (quiet grey).

props.name: checked
props.description: Whether the switch is currently active. To render an uncontrolled switch, use the `defaultChecked` prop instead.

props.name: className
props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: defaultChecked
props.description: Whether the switch is initially active. To render a controlled switch, use the `checked` prop instead.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Whether the component should ignore user interaction.

props.name: form
props.description: Identifies the form that owns the hidden input. Useful when the switch is rendered outside the form.

props.name: id
props.description: The id of the hidden input element. When `nativeButton` is `true`, the id is applied to the root element.

props.name: inputRef
props.description: A ref to access the hidden `<input>` element.

props.name: name
props.description: Identifies the field when a form is submitted.

props.name: nativeButton
props.description: Whether the component renders a native `<button>` element when replacing it via the `render` prop. Set to `true` if the rendered element is a native button.

props.name: onCheckedChange
props.description: Event handler called when the switch is activated or deactivated.

props.name: readOnly
props.description: Whether the user should be unable to activate or deactivate the switch.

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

props.name: required
props.description: Whether the user must activate the switch before submitting a form.

props.name: saving
props.description: Pending save: the handle shows a spinner, the switch is `aria-busy` and ignores clicks until it is cleared.

props.name: style
props.description: Style applied to the element, or a function that returns a style object based on the component's state.

props.name: uncheckedValue
props.description: The value submitted with the form when the switch is off. By default, unchecked switches do not submit any value, matching native checkbox behavior.

props.name: value
props.description: The value submitted with the form when the switch is on. By default, switch submits the "on" value, matching native checkbox behavior.

keyboard: Space / Enter: turn on or off
aria: role=switch with aria-checked
Needs a label: Label or Field

parts.name: Switch
parts.description: The track, with the switch role: 32 by 18 px by default, 24 by 14 px small. Grey when off, brand, neutral or muted when on, with a hit area that reaches 12 px sideways and 8 px up and down.

parts.name: Thumb
parts.description: The round knob, which slides with a slight overshoot and reverses mid-way if clicked again. While saving it shows a spinner, and Switch renders it for you.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The text that names the setting, a Label linked to the switch or the title of a Selector Item, and clicking it toggles the switch. Name the setting, never the state.

parts.name: SwitchItemCell
parts.description: A table cell that puts a Switch and its text in one label, so the text also toggles it.

items.text: Use it for one setting that is on or off and takes effect at once, such as email notifications. For a choice that is saved later with a form, use a Checkbox.
Give every switch a visible label and link it to the switch. A click on the text then toggles it, and a screen reader announces the name with on or off.
Name the setting, not the state: Email notifications, not On. The switch role already tells screen readers whether it is on.
Set the saving state while a request runs. The knob shows a spinner and clicks are ignored until the save ends.
When a save fails, set the switch back to its previous value and say so in a message with a retry, like Couldn't save. Try again.
Use the small size in dense rows such as table cells, and the default size in forms and settings.
Don't mark a switch invalid. It has no wrong value, and a failed save is an error of the request, so put it in the message.
Don't use a Switch to choose between two named options such as Monthly and Yearly. That is a choice, not on or off, so use a Radio Group.
Don't ask people to press a Save button after a Switch. A switch that waits for a button is a Checkbox.

props.description: Style applied to the element, or a function that returns a style object based on the component's state.

props.name: tone

keyboard: Arrow keys: move to and select the next or previous option
Tab: into and out of the group
aria: role=radiogroup with role=radio items; label the group (Fieldset legend or aria-label)

parts.name: RadioGroup
parts.description: The group: a radio group that holds the chosen value and lays the options out in a grid with an 8 px gap. Name it with an aria-label, and mark the whole group invalid if needed.

parts.name: RadioGroupItem
parts.description: One round option, 16 px across, with its own value. Its hit area reaches 12 px to the sides and 8 px above and below the circle, so a near miss still selects it.

parts.name: Dot
parts.description: The 6 px dot shown while the option is chosen. RadioGroupItem renders it; you do not pass it.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The text that names the option, a Label whose htmlFor matches the radio's id, or the title of a Selector Item. A click on it chooses the option.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: A line of detail under the label, in secondary text, such as when an order arrives. It is not part of the label, so it does not widen the name.

items.text: Use a Radio Group when people choose exactly one option from a short list they should see at once. For a long list use a menu, and for options shown as buttons use a Radio Button Group.
Name the group with a visible label and aria-labelledby, or with an aria-label. A screen reader announces the name when focus enters the group.
Give every option a visible label and join it with htmlFor and id, so a click on the text also chooses it.
Choose a sensible default when one exists. Once an option is chosen it cannot be cleared, so an empty start only helps when the choice is required.
Put the error on the group: mark it invalid and write one message under it. Do not repeat the message on every row.
Use Selector Item with a RadioGroupItem as its control when each option needs a title, a description and a price, such as plans.
Don't use two radios for on and off. A single setting that is on or off is a Switch or a Checkbox.
Don't validate before the first try. A red group on load reads as a mistake that was not made yet.
Don't split one choice into several groups, or put an unrelated control between the options. People expect the arrow keys to stay inside one group.

items.text: Use an Input for one line of free text: a name, an email address, a search term. Use a Textarea for several lines, and a Select or Combobox for a choice from a known list.
Give every Input a visible label. A placeholder disappears with the first keystroke and is not a name; a search field may use an aria-label.
Pick the type and autocomplete that match the value (email, password, cc-number). The browser then offers the right keyboard and fills the field in.
Mark a wrong value with an error and say what to do: Enter an email address like name@company.com, not Invalid input. Keep what the person typed.
Show the error after the person leaves the field or sends the form, not on the first keystroke. A red field on load reads as a mistake that has not been made yet.
Keep the label a noun (Work email) and put the rule in the helper below it as a full sentence.
Make every password field that a person types by hand revealable, and set autocomplete to current-password on sign-in or new-password on sign-up.
Don't import TextField or PasswordField in new code. They are deprecated aliases of Input; use Input with the same props.
Don't use a placeholder as the label, and don't put the format example only there: it is gone once the field is filled.
Don't size a field with height classes. Use the size prop (sm, default, lg), so a field and a Button of the same size line up in both densities.
Don't disable a value people need to read or copy. A read-only field can be focused and copied; a disabled one can't, and it is dimmed.
Don't use a number input for codes, phone numbers or card numbers. Use text with numeric input mode, so leading zeros survive.

items.text: Use it for free text over several lines: a message, a description, feedback. One line goes in an Input, formatted text in a Rich Text Editor.
Give it a visible label. A placeholder disappears with the first keystroke and isn't a name.
Set a maximum length together with show count when there is a limit. The counter needs both, and the field stops accepting text at the limit.
Say what to do in the error, such as Enter at least 20 characters, and keep what the person typed. Show it after they leave the field or send the form.
Pick the size for the text you expect: small for a note, default for a message, large for a description. People can still drag the field taller.
Mark the exception, not the rule. When most fields are needed, flag the few optional ones instead of putting a star on every other label.
Don't import TextareaField in new code. It is a deprecated alias, so use Textarea with the same props.
Don't size it with rows or height classes. Pick a size instead, because the heights follow density and stay right in compact and comfortable.
Don't hide the counter and cut the text off silently. A limit people can't see feels like a bug.
Don't put a chat composer's buttons next to the field by hand. Put the field and its buttons in one box that owns the border and focus ring.

items.text: Use Progress for a task that runs to completion: an upload, an import, a run of setup steps. For a fixed value inside a range, such as storage used, use Meter.
Name the bar with a label, such as Uploading report.pdf. Screen readers then say what is progressing, not only the number.
Add the value part when the number matters. It formats the value in tabular figures, so the text does not jump while it counts.
Put the value where it is read first: right for a compact row, bottom when the bar spans the full width, or a bubble when the number should follow the end of the fill.
Set the max to the number of steps when the task has steps, and pass the steps done as the value, such as 3 of 5. The bar then needs no sum of its own.
When you print your own text, also pass a value text for screen readers, such as 3 of 5 steps. Otherwise it announces the percent.
Say a failure in words next to the bar and offer the next action, such as Failed, retry. The bar keeps the value where the task stopped.
Don't animate the width of the fill yourself. The indicator already scales smoothly.
Don't use an indeterminate bar for a long wait on its own. It draws no fill and no motion, so pair it with a Spinner or a message.
Don't show a bar for a measured value such as storage used, since it would announce a task that is never finished. Use Meter.

parts.name: Slider
parts.description: Holds the value and draws one thumb per value: a number gives one thumb, an array of two gives a range. It offers several thumb styles, a centred fill, a value bubble, tick marks and an error state.

parts.name: SliderLabel
parts.description: A visible name for the slider, linked to the thumbs, placed with the value in a row inside the Slider. SliderField draws its own label.

parts.name: SliderValue
parts.description: Shows the current value or range on the right in tabular figures.

parts.name: SliderControl
parts.description: The area that takes pointer input, a little taller than the track so it is easy to hit. Slider already renders it.

parts.name: SliderTrack
parts.description: The grey bar the thumbs travel on, 6 px thick, horizontal or vertical. Slider already renders it.

parts.name: SliderIndicator
parts.description: The filled part of the track up to the value, or between the two thumbs of a range. A centred slider fills from its origin.

parts.name: SliderThumb
parts.description: The handle people drag or move with arrow keys, Home, End, Page Up and Page Down, and the element screen readers announce. It takes the page tone on hover and the subtle tone while dragging.

parts.name: SliderBubble
parts.description: The decorative value bubble above the thumb. It fades in on focus and while dragging, and thumbs close together share one.

parts.name: SliderMarks
parts.description: Decorative tick marks on the scale. Label only the marks that need a word, never every step.

parts.name: SliderField
parts.description: A slider as a form field: a label that names the thumbs, the current value with its unit, optional limits, number inputs and helper or error text. An error turns the slider red.

parts.name: SliderInput
parts.description: A number field that follows the slider, uses the English number format, and clamps and snaps when you leave it.

parts.name: SliderRangeInputs
parts.description: Two number fields for a range. The lower value may not pass the upper one.

items.text: Use it when the rough position matters more than the exact figure: volume, a price range, a zoom level. For an exact number use a Number Field.
Use SliderField for every slider in a form or panel, so the label and current value always sit next to the thumb. Add number inputs when exact values matter.
Name every slider: SliderField takes a label and a bare Slider takes an aria-label. A range is announced as Budget, minimum and Budget, maximum.
Set the step to the precision people need and keep the large step at about ten steps. Shift with an arrow key, Page Up and Page Down move by the large step.
Pass an array such as 20 and 80 as the value for a range. The slider draws one thumb per value.
Label only the marks that need a word, such as the first, the default and the last. A label on every tick is noise.
Show an error through the error prop: the fill and thumb turn red and the text is announced. Say what to change, like Choose at least 10%.
When a slider is disabled, give the reason in the helper text. The value stays readable, and people shouldn't have to guess why they can't change it.
Don't add SliderThumb children for a range. The array decides how many thumbs there are.
Don't rely on colour alone for an error. The red fill comes with the error text and an invalid state for screen readers.
Don't use a vertical slider without a height. It fills its container's height, so a column without one gives the track nothing to stretch to.
Don't use a Slider for a choice between a few named options. Use a Segmented Control or a Radio Group.

keyboard: Tab between the page links, Enter to open
aria: nav with aria-label "Pagination"; the current page has aria-current

parts.name: Pagination
parts.description: A nav named Pagination with Prev and Next around numbered page buttons. You hold the page and change it in the page change handler; options are shape, current style and first and last buttons.

parts.name: Edge buttons
parts.description: The first-page and last-page buttons at the two ends, shown with the edges option. Each is an icon button named First page or Last page.

parts.name: Prev and Next
parts.description: Text buttons with a chevron: Prev is disabled on the first page and Next on the last. Below 640 px the text hides and the chevron stays, and screen readers still read the text.

parts.name: Page button
parts.description: A numbered button that goes to its page. The row always shows the first page, the last page and the pages around the current one.

parts.name: Current page
parts.description: The page you are on, marked as the current page. Primary fills it with the brand colour, subtle sets it on a quiet surface.

parts.name: Ellipsis
parts.description: Stands for the pages that are folded away. It is plain text, not a button.

parts.name: PaginationSimple
parts.description: The compact form: Previous and Next with a Page X of Y label between them, for narrow spaces. It takes the same shape.

parts.name: PaginationSummary
parts.description: The count line: a range of a total (21 to 30 of 248), the total alone, a range without a total, a loading skeleton, or an error with a Retry button.

parts.name: PaginationPageSize
parts.description: A labelled select for the number of rows per page. Its label is the accessible name of the select.

parts.name: PaginationJump
parts.description: A labelled number field with a Go button. Enter or Go jumps to the page; a value outside 1 to the page count shows an error under the row.

items.text: Keep the page in state and load the matching rows in the page change handler. Pages count from 1, and the page count is the total number of pages.
Show where people are with PaginationSummary next to the pager, such as 21 to 30 of 248. When the total is unknown, leave it out and it says Showing 21 to 30.
Reset the page to 1 when the page size, a filter or a search changes. Otherwise people can land on a page that no longer exists.
Use PaginationSimple where only Previous and Next fit, such as a narrow card or a phone, and keep the count in PaginationSummary above the list.
Don't build page buttons by hand. Pagination already disables Prev on the first page and Next on the last, and marks the current page.
Don't show a pager for one page. With a page count of 1 it shows a lone 1; hide it instead.
Don't use Pagination for a feed that grows as people read. A list that appends more rows needs a Load more button or an infinite list, not pages.
Don't let the page leave the range 1 to the page count. Pagination does not clamp it, so a stale page shows a row with no current number.

parts.name: Separator
parts.description: A 1 px line, horizontal by default and as wide as its container, or vertical and as tall as its row. It can be dashed, never shrinks in a flex row and has no margin.

items.text: Use it to divide groups inside one surface, such as two sections of a card. For a line with text like or use Divider with Label, and inside a toolbar use ToolbarSeparator.
Place a vertical Separator in a flex row that has a height. It stretches to the row, so without one the line has nothing to stretch to.
Use the dashed style for a lighter break inside one section, such as the line above a total, and the solid line between sections.
Leave the spacing to the layout: a vertical margin between sections, padding on list rows, and a gap in a row.
Make the line decorative when a heading, list or group already shows the boundary. Keep the default when the line is the only sign of it.
Don't draw dividers with a border class or a hex colour. Separator uses the border token, so it follows the theme and dark mode.
Don't use a Separator as a panel resizer, because it is not focusable and has no value. A resizable layout needs a splitter with keyboard support.
Don't stack a Separator on a border that is already there, such as the last row of a bordered list or a card edge. Two lines read as one thick one.

components.title: Divider with Label
components.description: A separator with a centered text label, e.g. for "or" between two sign-in options.

parts.name: DividerWithLabel
parts.description: A full-width row of a line, a label and a second line, separating two groups such as two ways to sign in. A small size suits a short word like or, and the lines can be dashed.

parts.name: Lines
parts.description: Two decorative lines that stretch to fill the space on either side of the label. With no label the row itself becomes a single separator and the two lines meet in the middle.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: A word or two such as or, centred between the lines in muted text. It can also hold a small plain button, an icon button or an icon.

items.text: Use a Divider with Label between two alternative ways to do the same thing, such as social sign-in and email. For a line without text, use Separator.
Keep the label to one or two words that say how the groups relate: or, or continue with. Longer text squeezes the lines away.
Place it only between two alternatives, such as sign-in buttons above and an email form below. The label reads as a choice between what is above and what is below.
Use the small size for a one word label such as or, and the default size for a phrase such as or continue with.
Put a small plain Button or an IconButton on the line for an action that belongs to the break, such as Load more. Give an icon button an aria-label.
Use the same word as the buttons around it. If the buttons say Continue with, the label says or, not alternatively.
Don't use it as a section heading. The label is small, muted text with no heading role, so start a new section with a real heading.
Don't put it above the first or below the last block. It separates two blocks, so with only one side it points at nothing.

components.title: Skeleton
components.description: A pulsing placeholder shown while content is loading.

aria: Decorative: mark the loading region with aria-busy="true" and announce the result, not the skeleton

parts.name: Skeleton
parts.description: A grey placeholder with a soft sweeping highlight, as a 14 px text line, 20 px title line, 40 px avatar circle or 100 px block. It has no role or label and is still under reduced motion.

items.text: Use a Skeleton while content with a known layout loads: a list, a card, a profile. For a short wait on an action, such as saving, use a Spinner.
Give each Skeleton the size of the content it stands for. The layout then keeps its height and does not jump when the content arrives.
Make a text placeholder as tall as the line it stands for. The text shape is 14 px high and a normal line is 20 px, so add 3 px of margin above and below.
Draw what you already know, such as the table header or the card title, and put placeholders only where data is missing.
Mark the loading region as busy and remove that when the content is in. Add a visually hidden status line saying what is loading, because the placeholders say nothing to screen readers.
Show a skeleton for the first load only. When data refreshes, keep the old content on screen and update it in place.
Don't fill the whole screen with blocks. Cover what is visible when the page opens and let the rest render with its data.
Don't leave a skeleton on screen when loading fails. Replace it with an error message and a way to try again.
Don't build your own placeholder for charts. They have a loading state that draws a skeleton of the right height.

Esc: dismiss
aria: Supplementary only: never the only label of a control (icon buttons need aria-label)
a11y.notes: Opens after 600 ms on hover by default (delay).

parts.name: Tooltip
parts.description: Holds the open state and links the trigger to the label. You can control it, switch it off or leave it uncontrolled, and it renders nothing itself.

parts.name: TooltipProvider
parts.description: Shares one delay between the tooltips below it, for example in a toolbar. The first opens after 600 ms, and moving to another trigger within 300 ms shows its tooltip at once.

parts.name: TooltipTrigger
parts.description: The element the tooltip describes. It opens on hover and keyboard focus, and you pass your Button or IconButton and turn off the description if the tooltip repeats the trigger's name.

parts.name: TooltipContent
parts.description: The dark surface, drawn in a portal above the trigger by default, 8 px away. Side, alignment and offset move it and it flips near a viewport edge, long text wraps at 240 or 320 px, Escape closes it.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The tooltip's text: one short phrase in 12 px medium, white.

parts.name: Shortcut
parts.description: A key hint in its own dark chip after the label. Write it for the platform: ⌘K on macOS, Ctrl+K on Windows.

parts.name: Arrow
parts.description: The small point towards the trigger, which you can hide. It turns with the side the tooltip ends up on and keeps pointing at the middle of the trigger.

items.text: Use it for a short hint on a control: the name of an icon button, a shortcut, a truncated text in full. For content people read at length or act on, use a Popover.
Give the trigger its own name with an aria-label, since a tooltip adds information and is never a control's only label. Turn off the description when it repeats that name.
Keep the text to one short phrase without a full stop. Longer text wraps at 240 px, or 320 px if allowed, and for more than three lines use a Popover.
Add a shortcut only if it works, and write it for the platform. Use the linger option for a confirmation like Copied to clipboard, which fades out slowly instead of snapping away.
Put a toolbar's tooltips in one TooltipProvider, so the delay is the same everywhere and moving along the buttons shows each tooltip at once.
Make the reason a control is disabled visible without hover, for example as helper text. The tooltip, on a wrapper that can take focus, then only repeats it.
Place the tooltip where it covers neither a neighbouring control nor the text of the row. Choose side and alignment for that, and let it flip near the edge.
Don't put links or buttons in a tooltip. It only opens on hover and focus of the trigger, so keyboard users can't reach them.
Don't make a tooltip the only place for an error, a confirmation or task-critical information. Touch and keyboard users may never see it.
Don't put a tooltip on text that isn't interactive. Nothing can take focus there, so a keyboard user never sees it.

items.text: Always include a DialogTitle, even when the design shows none. Without it the dialog has no name for screen readers.
Put the main action last and name it after its result: Send invite, Create project, not OK. Keep Cancel neutral next to it.
On a failed submit keep the dialog open and the input, and put the message on the field or in an Alert at the top of the body.
While the request runs, show the pending state on the primary action and disable the others. Close the dialog only after the server confirms.
Put long content in a scrollable DialogBody so the title and footer stay in view.
Don't confirm a destructive action in a Dialog, since a click outside closes it. An Alert Dialog closes only through a button or Escape.
Don't use a dialog to report that something worked. A saved state is a toast, and a dialog that needs a click to dismiss only adds a step.
Don't discard unsaved input silently when the dialog closes. Ask with an Alert Dialog on top, where Keep editing returns to the form.
Don't nest dialogs or use one for a long flow. More than four steps belong on a page.

parts.name: AlertDialog
parts.description: Holds the open state. Control it yourself, or leave it uncontrolled and let the trigger and buttons handle it.

parts.name: AlertDialogTrigger
parts.description: The element that opens the window, usually the button that starts the action. Focus returns to it when the window closes.

parts.name: AlertDialogContent
parts.description: The window, with its own portal and backdrop. It has no corner close button, so the footer buttons are the way out; the large size matches the 440 px Figma set.

parts.name: AlertDialogHeader
parts.description: Stacks the icon, the title and the description at the top of the window.

parts.name: AlertDialogIcon
parts.description: A 40 px tile with the icon above the title, in a default, warning or destructive tint. Without children it shows an alert circle, a warning triangle or a trash can.

parts.name: AlertDialogTitle
parts.description: Names the action and its object, like Delete project Northstar? It is the accessible name of the window.

parts.name: AlertDialogDescription
parts.description: Says what will be lost or cannot be undone. It is read out after the title.

parts.name: AlertDialogFeedback
parts.description: An announced message above the actions, as an error or warning: what failed, whether anything changed, what to do next.

parts.name: AlertDialogFooter
parts.description: The row of buttons. The last button in the markup sits on the right, or on top when the footer is stacked.

parts.name: AlertDialogCancel
parts.description: Closes the window without acting. Label it with the safe choice, such as Cancel or Keep editing.

parts.name: AlertDialogAction
parts.description: Confirms and closes on click. Primary by default, destructive for removals, or secondary for a third way out such as Discard changes.

parts.name: AlertDialogOverlay
parts.description: The dimmed, lightly blurred backdrop, already rendered by the content. Clicking it does nothing.

parts.name: AlertDialogPortal
parts.description: Moves the window to the end of the document. The content already uses it; you only need it for a custom window or container.

items.text: Name the object and the loss in the title, like Delete project Northstar, and put what goes with it in the description. Don't just ask Are you sure.
Repeat the action on the confirm button and make it destructive for deletions: Delete project after Cancel, so it ends up on the right.
Label the safe choice with what it does, like Keep editing or Cancel. When the action is hard to undo, focus starts on it.
For slow or failing actions, control the open state yourself. The action button closes the window on click, so prevent that, show the failure in the feedback area and turn the button into Retry.
Ask for a typed confirmation only for large deletions that cannot be undone, with a visible label, and never together with an acknowledgement.
Don't confirm with window.confirm. It cannot be styled or tested, while an Alert Dialog keeps the product's look, focus handling and button labels.
Don't use an Alert Dialog for a form or to report that something worked. A task with fields belongs in a Dialog, and success in a toast.
Don't ask for confirmation on routine actions that can be undone. Do them and offer Undo; a window for everything teaches people to click through.
Don't rely on a click outside or a corner close button to dismiss it. Neither exists here: the footer buttons and Escape are the way out.

parts.name: Collapsible
parts.description: Holds the open state and wraps the trigger and the panel. Appearance is row (a full-width trigger) or inline (a link-style trigger), and without it the trigger keeps the plus and minus box.

parts.name: CollapsibleTrigger
parts.description: The header, a button that reports whether it is expanded. It can show a leading icon, a second line, a summary while closed, a count badge and an indicator, and hover and press change its fill.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: The optional icon before the label. It is decorative and takes the text colour.

parts.name: Label

parts.name: Indicator
parts.description: The chevron that flips when the panel opens, or the plus and minus box. The default is the chevron in both appearances.

parts.name: CollapsibleRow
parts.description: Puts a control beside the trigger, never inside it. The action slot takes a button such as Edit.

parts.name: CollapsibleContent
parts.description: The panel. It opens on a grid-row transition, so nothing is measured, and sits 24 px below the trigger (16 px when nested), lined up with the trigger text.

parts.name: CollapsibleFeedback

items.text: Pick row for a section header and inline for a link-style trigger under running text. Use one appearance per group of triggers.
Name the trigger after what is hidden, like Advanced options or Shipping details. Keep the title the same when it opens, and let only the indicator change.
Use the summary for what people need while the panel is closed, like 3 items and the total, and the count for the number of things inside. The count must equal the rows in the panel.
Keep fields a form needs outside the closed panel. A collapsed panel is easy to skip, and an error inside it stays out of sight.
Show loading, empty and error content with CollapsibleFeedback and offer an action such as Retry.
Don't put buttons or links inside CollapsibleTrigger, which is a button itself. Put an action beside it with CollapsibleRow.
Don't nest more than one level. For deeper structures use a tree view or separate pages.
Don't add a height transition to CollapsibleContent. It already animates with motion tokens, and a second animation fights it.
Don't stack several collapsibles to build an FAQ or a settings list. That is an Accordion, which also closes the open row.

items.text: Give an icon-only Toggle an aria-label such as Bold. The pressed attribute announces the state, not the label.
Keep the label and icon the same in both states. A label that flips between Mute and Unmute makes a screen reader say the opposite of what the fill shows.

Hold the state yourself when something else on the page depends on it, such as a filtered list.
Don't use a Toggle to run a one-off action such as Export. An action that doesn't stay on is a Button.
Don't use separate Toggles for one choice among several, such as left, centre and right alignment. Use a Radio Button Group, which keeps exactly one option chosen and can't be cleared.

Give it a label that names the thing, such as Star Q3 report.pdf, when several stars share a screen.

Don't use it for a rating of 1 to 5 stars. Rating is the component for that.
Don't use it as an on or off setting. Switch and Toggle say that in words.

parts.name: Meter
parts.description: The root: a div with the meter role and its minimum, maximum and current value. Children such as the label and value render above the bar.

parts.name: MeterLabel
parts.description: Names what is measured. Without a label, give Meter an aria-label.

parts.name: MeterValue
parts.description: Prints the formatted value at the right, a percent of the range by default, in tabular figures. It is hidden from assistive technology because the meter already announces its value.

parts.name: MeterIndicator
parts.description: The fill in the brand colour. It glides to a new value over the ambient duration, and Meter already renders it.

parts.name: MeterTrack
parts.description: The grey bar behind the fill, 8 px high and fully rounded. Meter renders it; you need it only for a custom layout.

items.text: Use a Meter for a measured value inside a known range: storage used, a score, a quota. For a task that runs to completion, use Progress.
Name it with MeterLabel or aria-label. Screen readers announce the value, and without a name they cannot say what it measures.
Set max to the real limit and show the unit: 38 of 50 GB, not a bare 76%. Use the format option or your own text in MeterValue.
When you print your own text, also pass getAriaValueText so a screen reader hears the same words: 38 of 50 gigabytes. Otherwise it announces the percent.
Measure bars that belong together against the same max, as in a storage widget, so the fills can be compared.
Say in words what a full or nearly full meter means and what to do: All seats are in use.
Don't use Meter for task progress. A meter reads as a measurement, so a half-full upload would look like a fixed value: use Progress.
Don't expect the fill to change colour near the limit. Meter has no low, high or optimum ranges, so tell the person in the text.
Don't animate the fill width yourself. It already moves with a transform, which is cheaper and matches the other bars.

components.title: Kbd
components.description: Displays a keyboard key or shortcut, e.g. inside a search input.

parts.name: Kbd
parts.description: One key chip, 22 px high with a subtle fill, a border and a 4 px corner, holding a single key or a short symbol group like ⌘K. The inverse tone is a dark 18 px chip for surfaces like tooltips.

parts.name: KbdGroup
parts.description: Lines up several keys in a row with a 4 px gap. Its tone passes on to every direct Kbd child that has none of its own, and the separator is drawn between two keys.

parts.name: Separator
parts.description: The text between two keys: a plus for a combination, a word such as then for a sequence. It is muted on light surfaces, white on inverse, and absent after the last key.

parts.name: KbdHint
parts.description: The shortcut hint: key caps with a short label after them, for the foot of a command menu or next to a search field. The caps are 22 px high with a muted fill and 11 px text, the label is tertiary text. It replaces KeyboardHint.

items.text: Use Kbd to show a keyboard shortcut next to the action it triggers: in a menu item, a command palette, a tooltip, a search field or a shortcuts panel.
Put one key in each Kbd and join keys with KbdGroup. Use a plus separator when the keys read as one combination, such as Ctrl + Shift + P, and a word like then for a sequence.
Write the keys the way the platform labels them: ⌘, ⇧ and ⌥ on macOS, Ctrl, Shift and Alt on Windows. Keep one platform per list.
Use the inverse tone when the shortcut sits on a dark surface, and set it on the KbdGroup so every key follows. A Kbd wrapped in another element doesn't get the group's tone.
Set aria-keyshortcuts on the control the shortcut triggers. The chip is text for the eye; the attribute tells assistive technology.
Don't use Kbd for decoration or for text that is not a key. It is a hint, not a button, and it doesn't run the shortcut.
Don't list a shortcut that the app doesn't handle. A hint that does nothing erodes trust in every other hint.
Don't mix platforms in one list, such as ⌘S next to Ctrl+F. Read the platform and show one set.

components.title: Spinner
components.description: A spinning indicator for an in-progress loading state.

aria: role=status with aria-label "Loading" — pass your own label when more specific

parts.name: Spinner
parts.description: A Lucide loader icon that turns once a second, 16 px and muted by default, announced as Loading. Pass an aria-label to say what is loading, or hide it when a visible text already does.

items.text: Use it for a short wait tied to an action: a status line that saves, a panel that refreshes. When content with a known layout loads, use a Skeleton.
When the spinner stands alone, pass a specific aria-label such as Saving changes. The default Loading says nothing about what is happening.
Beside a visible text, hide the spinner from screen readers and make the text a status, so the change is announced once, not twice.
Match the size to its neighbours: 16 px for body text, 24 px for a row icon, 32 px for a panel. Use the primary colour for a wait the person started, and keep the muted default for background work.
Keep the space the spinner takes when it goes away, so the layout doesn't move. Give its row a fixed height or swap in an icon of the same size.
Don't put a Spinner inside a Button. A button has a pending state that draws the spinner, keeps its width and blocks a second press.
Don't swap a chart or list for a Spinner while it loads, because the area collapses and the layout jumps. Use a Skeleton of the same size.
Don't use a Spinner when you know how far along the task is. Show a Progress bar, so people can tell whether it is worth waiting.

parts.name: Toolbar
parts.description: A framed row with the toolbar role, a 1 px border, the card fill and a 12 px corner, with 4 px of padding and gaps. It is one tab stop with arrow keys between items, named with an aria-label.

parts.name: ToolbarGroup
parts.description: Keeps related buttons close together with a 2 px gap, such as the text styles. It has the group role, and disabling it disables every item inside.

parts.name: ToolbarButton
parts.description: A 32 px square button with an 8 px corner for one icon. It joins the roving focus, and becomes a toggle when you render it as one: a pressed one takes the indigo tint.

parts.name: ToolbarSeparator
parts.description: A 1 px line between two groups, 20 px long with 4 px of margin on each side. It runs across the toolbar, vertical in a horizontal one and horizontal in a vertical one.

parts.description: A 14 px text link in the toolbar that arrow keys reach like the buttons. Use it for a destination such as a help page, and a button for an action.

items.text: Use it for controls that act on one thing, such as the formatting buttons of an editor or the tools of a canvas. For joined buttons that switch a view, use a Button Group.
Name the toolbar with an aria-label, such as Text formatting, and give every icon-only button its own aria-label.
Sort buttons into groups with a separator between them, so related actions sit together and arrow keys still pass through the whole row.
Show a tooltip with the name and shortcut on every icon button, and wrap one toolbar's tooltips in one TooltipProvider so they share a delay.
Keep a toolbar to one row of 4 to 12 items. When you need more tools, move the least used behind an overflow button instead of letting the row scroll.
Don't add your own arrow-key handling or tabIndex to the items. The toolbar already moves focus between them, and Tab leaves it.
Don't swap a button for a menu, select or field without testing it with the keyboard. Only buttons, links and inputs of the toolbar take part in its roving focus.
Don't use a Toolbar to navigate between pages. Use tabs or a navigation bar, since a toolbar is for actions on the thing in front of the user.

items.text: Name destructive entries after the action and the object, and use the destructive variant: Delete project, not Delete. The colour is a second cue, never the only one.
Put the destructive entry last, after a separator, and the most used entries first.
Disable an entry that does not apply right now instead of removing it. Arrow keys still reach it, so screen reader users learn that the action exists.
Show a loading line while entries load and an empty line when there are none, with the content marked busy while loading. The menu never opens as an empty box.
Put the shortcut in the shortcut part and the binding in aria-keyshortcuts, so a screen reader says Copy without reading out the keys.
Don't put links to pages in a Dropdown Menu. It is a menu of actions; navigation belongs in the navbar menu or in plain links.
Don't use it to pick a value for a form field. A Select or a Combobox shows the chosen value in the field itself.
Don't pile up entries. Past seven or eight, split the menu into labelled groups, and never nest more than one submenu.

Set a width, such as 16 rem. Without one the panel is as wide as its widest line.
Wrap Cancel and Apply in the close part, so focus goes back to the trigger.
Put the trigger where people expect the content to belong, and align the panel so it stays inside the page at the screen edge.
Don't put a long form, a table or a multi-step task in a popover. Use a Dialog or a side panel when people need the room.

items.text: Name the table with a caption, or with an aria-label when the page heading already does. On a table that scrolls sideways, that name also labels the scroll region.
Right-align numbers, heading included, and use tabular figures so they line up and don't shift when they change. Text stays left.
Give amounts and quantities their unit. CurrencyCell adds the currency, and for other figures the column heading names the unit.
Show a missing value as an em dash and give screen readers the words No value. An empty cell looks like a mistake, and a 0 claims something the data doesn't.
Keep the header while the table loads, is empty or fails, and show the state where the rows go. The columns stay put, so nothing jumps when rows arrive.
Don't set row padding or heights by hand. Rows follow the density setting.
Don't make a row clickable when nothing inside it is. A row has no focus ring or key action, so put a link or button in the first cell.
Don't stack many columns on a phone. A sideways scroll hides the right-hand columns, so pick the few that matter or use a list.
Don't build sorting, filters or paging by hand around a Table. When people need them, use Data Table, which keeps that state for you.

items.text: Write short labels in sentence case, one or two words: Billing history, not Billing History.
Keep every tab in a row the same kind: all labels, all icons with labels, or all with counts.
Always start with a selected tab. Keep the value in state or in the URL when people should be able to come back to a tab.
Give the list an aria-label, such as Project sections, when a page has more than one row of tabs.
Keep the number of tabs small enough for a phone. The row scrolls sideways when it runs out of room, and a tab past the edge is easy to miss.
Don't use tabs to move between pages. Links that change the route are navigation with aria-current, not a tab list.
Don't add your own key handlers to the tabs. Arrow keys, Home and End already move between them, and Tab moves on into the panel.
Don't set heights on the list or tabs. Pick a size instead, which follows the density and matches the Button sizes.
Don't hide what people must read or do in a tab they may never open. Put required information outside the tabs.
