parts.description: The group: a native fieldset with the group role. By default it is a card with a thin border, 12 px corners and 16 px padding, and its legend is the accessible name of the group.

parts.name: FieldsetLegend
parts.description: The name of the group in 14 px semibold text. It can sit anywhere inside the fieldset, for example on a row with a note, and it dims with a disabled fieldset.

parts.name: Hint
parts.description: A line under the legend in 12 px tertiary text that states the rule. Link it to the fieldset so a screen reader reads it with the group.

parts.name: Controls
parts.description: The related controls: checkbox rows, a radio group or fields. Keep 12 px between rows of one kind and 16 px between columns.

parts.name: Legend note
parts.description: A word such as Required beside the legend, in 12 px tertiary text. It is for sighted readers, so put the rule itself in the hint where a screen reader hears it.

parts.name: Group error
parts.description: One message under the controls that says what to do, with a 14 px alert icon. Link it to the fieldset and mark the fieldset as invalid: the card then takes the red border and tint.

items.text: Use a Fieldset when several controls answer one question: a set of checkboxes, the radios of one choice, the fields of an address. One control with its own label needs a Field.
Write the legend as the question or the noun of the group, such as Notification channels or Shipping address. It is read before every control, so keep it short.
State the rule in a hint under the legend and link it to the fieldset. Say it before the person breaks it: Choose where we send alerts.
Show one error for the group, not one per control, and say what to do: Select at least one option to continue. Show it after the first try to continue, and keep what was chosen.
Use the plain surface when the group sits straight on the page, and the card when it must stand apart, such as an address block in a long form.
To switch a group off, disable the Fieldset. For a checkbox or radio group also disable the control, or wrap each in a Field, because only Fields read the Fieldset.
Don't use a Fieldset to draw a box around unrelated content. It names a group for assistive technology; use a Card for a visual container.
Don't nest a Fieldset in a Fieldset to indent. Nest only when the inner group has a name of its own.
Don't leave the legend out and put the question in a heading next to the group. The group then has no name for a screen reader.

items.text: Use a Form for everything a person sends together. A single field that acts at once, like a search box, needs no Form, and a setting that applies immediately is a Switch.
Give every Field a name and handle the send in the submit handler. It gets the values by name and only runs when every field is valid, so Enter and the Save button take the same path.
Say what to do in the message: Enter a work email address, like name@company.com, not Invalid input. Show it under the field and keep what the person typed.
After a failed send, move focus to the first invalid field, and add an error summary to long forms. The summary jumps to each field and never replaces the message at the field.
Show the work: a pending Save with its own label (Saving…), the way out disabled, and a confirmation when done. Say All changes saved in the status line, not only with colour.
Keep the default: validate on submit, then re-check as the person corrects. Validate on blur for fields that are costly to get wrong, such as an address.
Don't disable the submit button to flag an invalid form, since it gives no reason. Let the person press it and tell them what is wrong; disable it only when there is nothing to send.
Don't clear the fields after an error or a server failure. Name the problem, keep the entries and offer Try again.
Don't run the check from a click handler on the submit button. Use the submit handler so keyboard and mouse users take the same path.

items.text: Use an Input Group when something belongs inside the field's border: an icon, a fixed part of the value or a small action on it. Other actions are buttons beside the field.
Put the input as a direct child of the group. The group styles direct child inputs and can't reach one wrapped in another element.
Keep the corners concentric. A 32 px IconButton in a 36 px group sits 2 px inside the border, so give it a 6 px corner and trim the group's padding on that side.
Name the button with aria-label and use aria-pressed for a toggle such as show or hide. An icon alone is not a name.
Set aria-invalid and disabled on the input, not on the group. The group reads them and turns the border red or dims itself.
For the other sizes, give the group a height class for the small or large field height. The inner button stays 32 px, so use it in the default and large sizes.
Don't put the main action of a form inside the field. Apply, Send and Subscribe are buttons of their own, next to the field.
Don't put a second field or a long text in an addon. An addon is a unit, an icon or a short word.
Don't rely on the addon text for the field's name. https:// is part of the value; the field still needs a Label.

parts.description: The visible name of the field: a Label whose htmlFor matches the NumberField id, so a click on it focuses the input. A field with no room for a label takes an aria-label on the input.

parts.name: NumberField
parts.description: The root. It holds the number (null when empty), the limits, the steps and the format, and it has no element of its own; its id goes on the input.

parts.name: NumberFieldGroup
parts.description: The bordered frame around the buttons and input: 36 px high, 8 px corner, 1 px dividers. It carries the hover border, the indigo focus ring and the red error state.

items.text: Give the field a visible label joined by htmlFor and the NumberField id. Where a column header already names it, put an aria-label on the input.
Set min, max and step to the real limits, such as 1 to 50. The buttons stop at the edges and Home and End jump to them.
Name the buttons after what they change, such as Add a seat and Remove a seat. The defaults, Increase and Decrease, do not say what grows.
Put the unit in the format (for example kilograms) or in the label, so the number is never read without it. Widen the input when the formatted text is longer than 64 px.
Treat the value as a number or null. A field the person emptied reports null, not 0; show an error under it and mark the input invalid.
Don't use it for a number nobody steps in small amounts, such as a year or a phone number. Use an Input with a numeric keyboard.
Don't use it for a count of one to ten where there is no typing. Number Stepper is a smaller control for that.
Don't leave the input without a name. The buttons have names; the input needs a label or an aria-label.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The visible name of the code: a Label whose htmlFor matches the OtpField id. It names the group and the first slot, and a click on it focuses the field.

parts.description: The group of slots: it holds the code as one string, moves focus and reports when the last slot is filled. A hidden input submits the code with the form.

parts.description: One slot per character: a native input, 40 px square with an 8 px corner. Only one slot is in the tab order, so give every slot after the first an aria-label such as Digit 2 of 6.

items.text: Use an OTP Field for a short code typed once: an email or SMS code, an authenticator code, a PIN. For dashed codes, long letter codes or a recovery key, use an Input.
Render one OtpFieldInput per character and set the same number as the length. A six-digit code needs six slots.
Give the field a visible Label whose htmlFor matches the id, and name every slot after the first with an aria-label such as Digit 2 of 6, so a screen reader announces the position.
Leave autoComplete at its one-time-code default, so a phone offers the code from the message. The first slot takes the paste and spreads it across the slots.
Check the code in the complete handler, or turn on auto-submit inside a form. The person should not have to find a button after the last digit.
Say what to do when a code fails, with a message like That code is not correct, or one for an expired code with a Resend action. Keep what was typed so one digit can be fixed.
Don't change the length while the person is typing, and don't mix code lengths in one field. Render another field instead.
Don't use an OTP Field for a long or free-form value. A long code is hard to check by eye in slots; use an Input.
Don't use real or reused codes in examples, tests or screenshots. Use demo values such as 470921.

parts.name: Combobox
parts.description: The root. It holds the chosen value, the typed text, the items and the filter, and the value is an item or null, or an array with multiple.

parts.name: ComboboxInputGroup
parts.description: The bordered frame around the input and the chevron, 36 px high with an 8 px corner. It draws the border and focus ring, dims when disabled and turns red when the input is invalid.

parts.name: ComboboxInput
parts.description: The text input: typing filters the list, arrow keys move through it, Enter chooses and Escape closes. Give it a visible label or an aria-label.

parts.name: ComboboxTrigger
parts.description: The chevron button that opens and closes the whole list. It is named Show options and is not in the tab order, because the keyboard opens the list from the input.

parts.name: ComboboxPopup
parts.description: The list panel. It brings its own portal and positioner, matches the width of the field and scrolls when it runs out of room.

parts.name: ComboboxList
parts.description: Renders the entries. Pass a render function as the child, so the filtered list, not the full one, is mapped, and with groups it receives one group at a time.

parts.name: ComboboxGroup
parts.description: Holds the entries of one group under a group label. A group without a match disappears with its label.

parts.name: ComboboxGroupLabel
parts.description: The heading of a group, in 12 px medium muted text. It is not an entry, so arrow keys skip it.

parts.name: ComboboxItem
parts.description: One entry, 32 px high for a single line, whose value is what the field holds when chosen. A row can hold an icon, or an avatar and a second line, and the highlighted row takes the page fill.

parts.name: Check
parts.description: A 16 px check at the right of the chosen entry. With multiple, every chosen entry shows one.

parts.name: ComboboxEmpty
parts.description: A centred line shown in place of the list when nothing matches. It is hidden while it has no content.

parts.name: ComboboxPortal
parts.description: Moves the list to the end of the document. The popup already renders it, so you only need it for a custom container.

items.text: Give the input a visible label that points at it. The placeholder is a hint such as Search projects, not the name of the field.
Always include an empty-state line with a sentence such as No projects match, so a list without matches never looks broken.
Keep the state as a value or null. It is null while nothing is chosen and after the choice is cleared.
With multiple, show the chosen entries next to the field, as a count or a list. The field only shows what people type.
Group a long list by what people already know, such as an area or a team, and pass the groups as the items.
Don't use it for free text. Text that is not an entry is dropped when the field loses focus, so use an Autocomplete when any value is valid.
Don't use it for a short list people can see at a glance. A Select is quicker when there are about a dozen options or fewer.
Don't turn on multiple and then hide the choices. People cannot tell what is selected from a closed field with a placeholder.

parts.description: The root. It holds the field's text, the items and the filter and renders nothing itself; the value is the text in the input, not a chosen item.

parts.description: The bordered frame around the input, 36 px high with an 8 px corner. It draws the border and focus ring, dims when disabled and turns red when invalid, so put an icon beside the input inside it.

parts.description: The text input. Typing filters the suggestions, arrow keys move through them, Enter takes one and Escape closes the list; give it a visible label or an aria-label.

parts.name: AutocompletePopup
parts.description: The suggestion panel. It brings its own portal and positioner, matches the field's width and scrolls when it runs out of room.

parts.description: Renders the items. Pass a render function as the child so the filtered list, not the full one, is mapped.

parts.name: AutocompleteItem
parts.description: One suggestion, 32 px high for a single line, whose value fills the field when chosen. A row can hold an icon, or an avatar and a second line, and the highlighted row gets the page fill.

parts.name: AutocompleteEmpty
parts.description: A centred line shown in place of the list when nothing matches. It is hidden while it has no content.

items.text: Give the input a visible label. The placeholder is a hint such as Search cities, not the name of the field.
Always add an empty-state line with a sentence like No cities match, so a list without matches never looks broken.
Control the value with state when the text drives something else, such as a server search. The value is the text of the field, never an item object.
Keep the suggestions few, five to eight, and one line each. Cap a long list with a limit; people pick by reading, so rows with several lines or controls slow them down.
Don't treat the value as validated. Text that matches no suggestion still ends up in the value, so check it on submit or use a Combobox.
Don't use it for a choice that must come from the list. A Combobox keeps the field on a value of the list and tells people when nothing matches.
Don't use it as a menu of actions. Suggestions fill a field; actions belong in a Dropdown Menu.

keyboard: Tab: into the day grid once (selected day, today or the first day) and to the month buttons

parts.description: An inline month grid, Monday first, for a single day or a range, with 32 px or 40 px days. For a field with a popover, use DatePicker.

parts.name: CalendarHeader
parts.description: The month title between the previous and next buttons, as a plain label or two buttons that open the month and year picker. A hidden arrow keeps its slot, so the title stays centred.

parts.name: Weekday labels
parts.description: Seven weekday labels, Mo to Su, each read as the full weekday by screen readers. The grid always shows six weeks, so its height never changes.

parts.name: CalendarDay
parts.description: One button per day: selection, today, outside days and unavailable days describe the date, while hover, pressed and focus describe the pointer. The figure marks the start of a range.

parts.name: Range band
parts.description: In range mode, days between start and end form one connected tint band with filled, rounded ends. While only the start exists, hovering a later day previews the band.

parts.name: Marked day
parts.description: A dot under the number of a day that has data, such as an event or an open slot. The dot is never the only cue: a label is added to the day's accessible name.

parts.name: Today
parts.description: Today has a ring on top of any selection. You can override today's date, which helps in demos and tests.

parts.name: CalendarPeriodPicker
parts.description: A 3 by 4 grid of months or twelve years with its own previous and next buttons. It opens from the month and year header and also works on its own.

parts.name: Restriction
parts.description: A blocked day can show its reason in a tooltip and in its accessible name. A loading, empty or error status blocks every day, and the banner that explains it sits next to the calendar.

parts.name: CalendarPeriodCell
parts.description: One month or year button in the period picker.

items.text: Use Calendar to show a month inline, next to a schedule or in your own popover. To pick a date in a form field, use DatePicker.
In range mode the first click sets the start, the second the end, and a third starts a new range. A range without an end is a draft, so say in the interface what is missing.
Use the larger size (40 px days) when the calendar is the main control and the smaller one (32 px) in dense panels.
Use the month and year header for birth dates and other far dates, so nobody pages month by month. Set the starting month, or control the month when two calendars must move together.
Limit the choice with a minimum and maximum, and block single days with a list or a rule such as weekends. Say why in a tooltip or in the text nearby.
Mark days that carry data and name the meaning, for example has events or has open slots.
While data loads or fails, set the status and show a banner beside the calendar that explains why and offers a retry.
Don't rely on a dot alone to show that a day has events. Name its meaning and list the events next to the calendar.
Don't show hover, pressed or the range preview as a confirmed choice. A confirmed day never changes on hover, and the preview band is lighter.
Don't block days without saying why. Screen readers announce a blocked day as unavailable, but a sighted person sees only a dimmed number.

components.title: Date Picker
components.description: A Calendar inside a Popover, with Cancel/Apply actions.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Days that cannot be picked: a list of dates or a test (passed to Calendar).

props.name: max
props.description: Latest day that can be picked (passed to Calendar).

props.name: min
props.description: Earliest day that can be picked (passed to Calendar).

props.name: numberOfMonths
props.description: Months shown side by side. Defaults to 2 for range mode.

props.name: presets
props.description: Quick-select sidebar (Figma: Type=presets). `true` uses the built-in presets.

keyboard: Enter / Space on the trigger: open the calendar
In the calendar: the Calendar date-grid keys (arrows, Home / End, Page Up / Page Down, Enter)
Esc: close
aria: Give the trigger an accessible name (aria-label or a Field label)
min, max and disabled reach the Calendar: blocked days are aria-disabled

parts.name: DatePicker
parts.description: The trigger and the popover in one component. It looks like a plain button or, as a field, adds a label, a format hint and an error line, and it picks a single date or a range.

parts.name: Trigger
parts.description: The element that opens the popover: a button, a field, or a text field you can type in. It shows Pick a date or the format hint while empty, then the chosen date or range.

parts.name: DatePickerPanel
parts.description: The popover content: calendars, presets and footer. A range shows two months side by side, a single date one, and the popover is as wide as its content (312 px for one month).

parts.name: Presets
parts.description: A column of quick ranges at the left, such as Last 7 days. Use the eight built-in ones or your own; choosing one fills the draft and Apply still confirms.

parts.name: Calendar
parts.description: A medium Calendar with its own header and arrows: two calendars for a range, one for a single date. See the Calendar page for its keys and states.

parts.name: Summary
parts.description: The line at the left of the footer. It says what is missing, explains an error, or shows the choice, with the length of a range in days or nights.

parts.name: Cancel and Apply
parts.description: Cancel closes the popover and drops the draft. Apply commits it and closes, and stays disabled while nothing valid can be committed.

parts.name: DatePickerField
parts.description: The closed field alone, without a popover, with its label and helper line. It is what the picker draws as a field, and is useful next to an inline panel.

parts.name: DatePickerFooter
parts.description: The summary line with Cancel and Apply, as its own part for panels you compose yourself.

items.text: Use the default button for a filter in a toolbar, and the field in a form, where it needs a label, a hint and an error line.
Let people type dates far in the past or future, such as a date of birth. Typing beats paging, and the field takes MM/DD/YYYY or a written date like Nov 12, 2026.
Use range mode with presets for reporting, where people usually want Last 7 days or Month to date. The picker shows one month below 830 px on its own.
Use instant confirmation for a single date that is easy to change, such as a due date. Keep Apply and Cancel for ranges and for dates that trigger work, such as a booking.
Limit the choice with min, max and disabled days. They block days in the calendar and are enforced when a date is typed.
Say what an unfinished or invalid range needs. The field shows Select an end date to finish the range, or the error, and Apply stays off until the range is valid.
Don't use instant confirmation with a range. Without the footer there is nothing to commit it.
Don't use a Date Picker for a month shown next to your content. Use Calendar, which has no popover.
Don't leave the label out of a field. The format hint disappears once a date is chosen, but the label stays.

components.title: Alert
components.description: An inline banner in 5 colors and 2 sizes, with an optional close button and action.

props.name: icon
props.description: Replaces the leading icon (default: a check circle, a warning triangle for negative and warning; with `size="inline"` a shield check). `null` hides it.

aria: Has role="alert", so a screen reader announces it when it appears on the page. A message that is already there on load is not read out; for a short confirmation after an action use a toast

parts.name: Alert
parts.description: The banner, with role alert. It comes in five variants (plain, positive, primary, negative, warning) and two sizes (large, small), and picks its icon from the variant. With size inline it is a static line of text without a box and without the role.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: The leading icon: a check circle, or a warning triangle for negative and warning. You can replace it or hide it.

parts.name: AlertTitle
parts.description: The bold first line. In the small size it stays on one line and truncates only when the banner is very narrow.

parts.name: AlertDescription
parts.description: The message. In large it wraps under the title; in small it takes the rest of the line and ends in an ellipsis.

parts.name: Close button
parts.description: A native button named Dismiss, drawn only when a close handler is set.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: Any Button after the description, usually plain and small. In large it sits under the text; in small it ends the row.

items.text: Say what happened in the title and what to do next in the text, like Changes couldn't be saved and Check your connection and try again.
Pick the colour for the meaning: positive for done, negative for failed, warning for attention, primary for information and plain for a neutral note.
Place the alert next to what it is about: under the field that failed, or at the top of the section it describes.
Give an alert that is only information a close button, and keep one that blocks people on the page until the cause is fixed.
Don't use an alert for a confirmation that should vanish by itself. A Toast fits a short message after an action.
Don't stack more than two or three alerts. Merge them into one, or move the details into a list.
Don't rely on the colour alone. The title and the text must say what happened, because not everyone sees the colour.
Don't put long text or a form in an alert. Link to a page for the details.

components.title: Toast
components.description: A temporary notification that appears in the corner of the screen, with success/error/warning/info types.

props.name: position
props.description: Corner the stack lives in.

props.name: limit
props.description: The maximum number of toasts that can be displayed at once. When the limit is exceeded, the oldest toasts are marked as `limited` (via the `data-limited` attribute) rather than removed, so they can be hidden or animated out.

props.name: timeout
props.description: The default amount of time (in ms) before a toast is auto dismissed. A value of `0` will prevent the toast from being dismissed automatically.

props.name: toastManager
props.description: A global manager for toasts to use outside of a React component.

props.name: className
props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

props.name: style
props.description: Style applied to the element, or a function that returns a style object based on the component's state.

keyboard: Toasts do not take focus; the close button is reachable with Tab
aria: Announced to screen readers through the Base UI toast live region
The close button is labelled "Close"

parts.name: Toaster
parts.description: The one-line setup. It wraps your app in a provider, renders the viewport and draws every toast, and you pick the corner: top right or bottom right.

parts.name: ToastProvider
parts.description: The provider on its own, with a default timeout of 5000 ms and a stack limit of 3 toasts. Toaster already includes it.

parts.name: ToastViewport
parts.description: The fixed region in the corner, a live region labelled Notifications that holds the stack. Toaster already renders it.

parts.name: Toast
parts.description: One notification, a card with a border and a shadow. Older toasts sit smaller and fainter behind the newest, and hovering or focusing the stack spreads them into a list.

parts.name: Type dot
parts.description: A small dot showing the type: green for success, red for error, yellow for warning and indigo for info.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The bold first line that names the outcome, such as Settings saved.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: One line of detail under the title. It only appears when the toast has a description.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: A text button in the link colour, such as Undo. It only appears when the toast has action props with a label and a click handler.

parts.name: Close button
parts.description: A button named Close that closes the toast at once.

items.text: Write the title as the outcome in a few words, such as Settings saved. Use the description only for detail people need, like what to do next.
Offer Undo for actions people can take back, such as a delete, instead of asking them to confirm first.
Use the promise helper for work that takes a while, so one toast goes from loading to success or error.
Add the Toaster once, high in the app, and call the useToast hook only below it.
Don't use a toast for a problem people have to fix. It goes away, so keep an Alert on the page until the cause is gone.
Don't put information in a toast that appears nowhere else. It can be missed or closed, so the result must also show on the page.
Don't fire several toasts for one action. Merge them into one message, since the stack shows three at a time.
Don't make many toasts stay forever with a timeout of 0. Keep that for a warning people must act on.

components.title: Pull to Refresh
components.description: Drag down from the top of any content past a threshold to trigger an async refresh, with a rotating spinner and a rubber-band release.

props.name: onError
props.description: Called when `onRefresh` throws or its promise rejects. The indicator resets either way and the rejection is not left unhandled; without `onError` the failure is swallowed here, so show it in your own UI.

parts.name: PullToRefresh
parts.description: A clipping box around your content. Give it a height and a background, since the indicator sits behind the content and shows as it moves down.

parts.name: Indicator
parts.description: The spinner icon at the top of the box. It fades in and turns with the pull, then spins until the refresh settles.

parts.name: Content
parts.description: The wrapper around your content that moves down with the pull. It takes the pointer events, lets the browser keep scrolling the content up, and shows a grab cursor, so text inside cannot be selected.

items.text: Return the promise from the refresh handler. The spinner and the lock stay until it settles, so a slow request never looks finished.
Pass an error handler and show the failure in text, such as Couldn't refresh. The component resets after a failure but shows nothing itself, and without a handler the failure is swallowed silently.
Put a visible Refresh button beside the list that calls the same function. The gesture is pointer-based, with no keyboard route and no announcement.
Announce the result in a status line, such as Updated just now. The component says nothing to assistive technology.
Give the box a height, a background and content that fills it. The box clips what moves out of it, and its background shows behind the content during the pull.
Keep the threshold at or below the maximum pull (defaults 70 and 110). The pull moves at half the finger speed, so people drag about twice the threshold.
Don't make the gesture the only way to refresh. Many people use a keyboard, a switch or a screen reader, and on a desktop mouse the drag is easy to miss.
Don't use it for data that updates by itself. Show the new state instead and skip the gesture.
Don't put text people should select inside the content. A drag must not select text, so the content blocks selection and nothing there can be copied.
Don't expect a tap to work right after a pull. The click that ends a drag is swallowed on purpose, so the item under the finger is not opened.

components.title: Rating
components.description: An interactive star rating input.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Names the group ("Rating" by default); read-only, it replaces "Rated 3.5 out of 5".

props.name: aria-labelledby
props.description: Id of a visible label that names the group, instead of `aria-label`.

props.name: size
props.description: `sm`: the compact 12 px display of a read-only star or heart row. Ignored while the rating is interactive.

keyboard: Arrow Left / Right: change the rating
aria: Interactive: role=radiogroup with one role=radio per star; read-only: role=img with a label

parts.name: Rating
parts.description: The group of options. Interactive it is a radio group with one Tab stop, and read-only it is a single image that reads Rated 3.5 out of 5, named by an aria-label.

parts.name: Option
parts.description: One radio of the group: a star or heart (24 px), a face (48 px) or a scale number (40 px high). Hover previews the fill of stars and hearts, and a click or arrow key chooses.

parts.name: Filled icon
parts.description: A star in the yellow brand tone or a heart in the pink one, filled up to the value.

parts.name: Empty icon
parts.description: The outline in the control border colour for the options beyond the value.

parts.name: Value label
parts.description: The number beside the row, on the left or right. The tooltip option shows it in a dark bubble with an arrow above the chosen option instead.

parts.name: RatingCell
parts.description: A read-only star row with the value on the right, made for table cells.

items.text: Pick the type for the question: stars for an opinion, hearts for favorites, emojis for a mood, and scale for a 0 to 10 survey answer such as Net Promoter Score.
Give every interactive Rating a visible question and tie it with aria-labelledby, or set an aria-label. The default name is only Rating.
Set read-only when you display an average. A fractional value such as 3.5 fills the nearest icon and keeps the exact number in the accessible name.
Show the label on the right when the number matters. Without it, a score of 4.5 is only a row of icons.
Show a comment field after a low score, so people can say what went wrong. Send the score only when they confirm it.
Don't use the tooltip label against the top edge of a container. The bubble floats about 32 px above the row and takes no space in the layout, so leave room for it.
Don't expect hover to choose. It only previews the fill of stars and hearts; a click or arrow key chooses, and arrows move and choose in one step.
Don't use the emojis type for a required answer. Clicking the chosen face again clears it and sends 0.

components.title: Trend Chip
components.description: A small pill showing a change, up or down, in seven icon styles.

props.name: direction
props.description: Figma Trend Chip · Trend; `flat` is the old name for `neutral`.

props.name: icon
props.description: Figma Trend Chip · Icon; the same glyph turns for `down`. Default `arrow-diagonal`: up-right for a rise, down-right for a fall.

props.name: sentiment
props.description: Figma Trend Chip · Sentiment: whether the change is good or bad. `auto` colours by direction (up green, down red); use `positive` for a fall that is good (churn, cost) or `negative` for a rise that is bad. The arrow always follows `directi…

parts.name: TrendChip
parts.description: An inline span with a glyph and a label. It isn't interactive and holds no state, so you pass the finished label, the direction and, when colour shouldn't follow direction, the sentiment.

parts.name: Pill
parts.description: The rounded surface, 20 px high. Its colour comes from the sentiment: green tint for positive, red for negative, grey for neutral.

parts.name: Glyph
parts.description: One of seven icons. The same glyph turns for down and a neutral chip always shows a minus, and the glyph follows the text colour and is hidden from screen readers.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The value text in 12 px semibold. It is the only part a screen reader reads, so it carries the sign and the unit.

parts.name: TrendCaret
parts.description: The filled triangle behind the triangle icon, also used by the change label of Number Value. It is exported for your own layouts and is decorative.

items.text: Write the sign and unit into the value: +12.4%, -3 pts, +$1,204. The glyph is hidden from screen readers, so the label is all they get.
Keep direction and meaning apart. Direction sets which way the glyph points and sentiment sets the colour: falling churn is down and positive, a rising ticket count is up and negative.
Choose one icon style per screen and keep it. The padding follows the glyph, so mixed styles in a column don't line up.
Name what the change is measured against, in the chip (+4.2% vs last month) or in the text beside it. A change without a reference says little.
Don't leave sentiment on auto for a metric where a fall is good. Auto colours by direction, so a falling error rate would show red.
Don't rely on colour alone. Green and red don't reach everyone, so the sign in the label and the glyph direction say the same thing.
Don't use it for a status or a count. A chip shows a change, so for a state such as Paid or Failed use Badge.
Don't use flat as a direction in new code. It is the old name for neutral.

components.title: Pressable Feedback
components.description: Wraps any content with a scale-down press animation.

props.name: asChild
props.description: Apply the press effect to the child element instead of wrapping it.

parts.name: PressableFeedback
parts.description: Scales its content to 95 % at 90 % opacity while pressed. Alone it renders a button, with asChild it lends the effect to its single child, and it adds a focus ring only.

parts.name: Content
parts.description: What you pass as children: a label, an icon with a label, a card body. It scales together with the button.

items.text: Use it to give press feedback to something that is not a button yet, such as a tile, card or row. Buttons and icon buttons already react to a press.
Pass asChild when the child is already a button or a link. Without it you nest a button inside a button, which is invalid HTML.
Handle the action with the press handler. With asChild the child's own click handler runs first, then the press handler.
Give the pressable its own look: a border, a fill and a hover tone. The component only adds the scale, the opacity and the focus ring.
Don't put links or other buttons inside it without asChild. They would sit inside a button, and nested interactive elements break.
Don't use it for a disabled state or a name that is not in the content. Its own button takes neither; use asChild and put them on the child.
Don't use it on a large surface, such as a whole panel. A 5 % scale of a wide element moves its edges visibly.

components.title: Emoji Reaction Button
components.description: A toggleable emoji reaction with a count, like a Slack reaction.

props.name: emoji
props.description: The reaction as an emoji. Leave it out and pass `icon` where the product shows no emoji.

props.name: icon
props.description: The reaction as an icon (14 px, e.g. a thumbs up), in place of `emoji`.

props.name: label
props.description: What the reaction means ("Agree", "Thanks"): the accessible name is "<label>: <count>". Needed with an `icon`, which has no text of its own; `aria-label` replaces it entirely.

parts.name: EmojiReactionButton
parts.description: A native button that shows an emoji and a count and reports whether it is pressed. It is controlled: you hold the active state and count and change them in the toggle handler.

parts.name: Pill
parts.description: The 26 px high capsule with a 1 px border and a small gap between emoji and count. Off, it has a neutral border and secondary text; on, an indigo tint with indigo border and text.

parts.name: Emoji
parts.description: The emoji character, at the text size of the pill. It is part of the button's accessible name, so a screen reader reads the emoji and then the count.

parts.name: Count
parts.description: The number of people who reacted, shown as a plain number after the emoji. It does not change by itself when pressed, so update it in the toggle handler.

items.text: Keep the active state and the count together and change them in the toggle handler: turning on adds one, turning off takes one away.
Show only the reactions that exist, and open an Emoji Picker from a small icon button for the rest. A reaction that drops to zero should disappear.
Put the buttons in a wrapping row with a gap, so they wrap on a narrow screen instead of overflowing.
Don't use it as a general toggle. It is for a reaction with a count; for an on or off option in a toolbar use Toggle.
Don't show a count of zero. A reaction nobody has chosen is not shown, and the Emoji Picker adds it again.
Don't use an emoji as the only information. Where the meaning matters, say it in text near the buttons.
Where the product shows no emoji, pass an icon and a label; the label names the button ("Agree: 3").

components.title: Emoji Picker
components.description: A grid of selectable emoji, typically shown inside a Popover.

parts.name: EmojiPicker
parts.description: A panel with a grid of emoji buttons, in a group named Emoji. It keeps no state: it hands the pressed emoji to your handler and you decide what happens next.

parts.name: Panel
parts.description: The card around the grid: a border, the popover surface, a shadow and 16 px corners. Six columns with 4 px between them and 8 px of padding make a row 230 px wide.

parts.name: Emoji button
parts.description: A 32 px button with 8 px corners, named by its emoji. Hover fills it with the page tone, pressed with the subtle tone, and keyboard focus shows the indigo border and 2 px ring.

items.text: Put the picker inside a Popover opened by an icon button and close it on pick. The picker draws its own card, so strip the border, background, padding and shadow from the popover content.
Pass a short list of emoji in a fixed order. The grid has six columns, so 6, 12 or 18 emoji fill every row.
Give the trigger an accessible name such as Add a reaction. The picker names its own buttons by their emoji, but the button that opens it needs words.
Don't use it as an emoji keyboard. It shows only the emoji you pass: no search, categories, skin tones or recently used.
Don't use an emoji as the only information in a control. The buttons are named by the emoji alone, so keep visible text where the meaning matters.
Don't expect it to close anything. The picker does not know about the Popover it sits in, so a pick leaves it open until you close it.

components.title: Checklist Task
components.description: One step of an onboarding checklist that can be ticked off, with the next step to do highlighted.

props.name: action
props.description: A button shown on the current step, e.g. "Start".

props.name: current
props.description: The step to do next — tinted, with room for `meta` and an `action`.

props.name: onClick
props.description: Toggle the step.

parts.name: ChecklistTask
parts.description: The row: 12 px side padding, 8 px radius and 12 px between its parts. A done or open step is one checkbox button, while the current step is a tinted block with two buttons.

parts.name: Circle
parts.description: A 22 px circle: empty with a 1.5 px rim while open, indigo rim on the current step, solid green with a tick when done. On the current step it is its own checkbox button named Mark as done.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The label in 14 px medium text. It is quiet (tertiary) when the step is done and takes the tint of the row on the current step.

parts.name: Meta
parts.description: The meta line under the label, in 12 px text, for example the time a step takes. It is shown in every state.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: The action, usually a Start button, at the right of the current step. The other states do not render it.

parts.name: Chevron
parts.description: A 16 px chevron at the right of an open step that is not current. A done step and the current step have none.

items.text: Use Checklist Task for the steps of an onboarding or setup checklist. For a plain list of options without a next step, use Checkbox Field.
Mark exactly one step current and give it an action such as Start. Only the current step shows the action, and its circle becomes a checkbox button of its own.
Handle the click as a toggle. It fires for open and done steps alike, so a step can be ticked and unticked again.
Work out the current step from the list, as the first step that is not done, so it moves on by itself when a step is ticked.
Put the steps in a list. Inside a panel with 8 px of padding and a 16 px radius, the 8 px row is concentric to the panel.
After a tick, move focus back to the checkbox of the step that was pressed. The current step is rebuilt as another element, so a step that becomes or stops being current loses focus.
Don't pass an action to steps that are not current. It is not rendered there.
Don't use a step for something that cannot be ticked yet. There is no disabled state, so leave the step out until it can be done.

components.title: Text Link Row
components.description: A line of text followed by a link, like “Don't have an account? Sign up”, or a back link with an arrow.

props.name: text
props.description: Leading copy, e.g. "Don't have an account?"

props.name: link
props.description: Link label, e.g. "Sign up". Omitted for Type=back.

props.name: variant
props.description: inline (14px) · small (12px) · stacked (two lines, centered) · icon (help icon + small) · back (arrow, no link)

parts.name: TextLinkRow
parts.description: A paragraph that lays its children out in one flex line, centred, 4 px apart. It is as wide as its container, starts at the left and has no border or background.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: A 16 px help icon in front of the text, only in the icon variant. It sits 8 px from the text.

parts.name: Text
parts.description: The text in a span: 14 px secondary for inline, 12 px tertiary for small and icon, 14 px tertiary for stacked.

parts.name: Link
parts.description: The link, semibold in the link colour, 14 px (12 px in small and icon) and underlined on hover. Without a link no anchor is rendered.

items.text: Use it for the quiet line that points to the other way through an auth screen: sign up instead of sign in, resend, change the address, contact support, go back. The main step stays a Button.
Keep the text to one short sentence and the link to one or two words. The text states the situation and the link names where it leads, such as Don't have an account, then Sign up.
Give the link a real href when it goes somewhere, since the default scrolls to the top. For an action that stays on screen, like Resend, handle the click and change the text so people see it worked.
Centre the row under a centred card with justify-center. By default the row fills its container and starts at the left.
Use the back variant for the way out of a step, last on the screen. It carries only text, so a link passed with it is ignored.
Don't put a long sentence in the text. It wraps in its own column and squeezes the link, so in a narrow container let the link wrap under the text.
Don't use it for the main or a destructive action. A text link is easy to miss and has no pressed or loading state, so use a Button.
Don't leave the href at the default for a link you don't handle. The page jumps to the top and the history gets an entry.

components.title: Social Sign In Buttons
components.description: Sign-in buttons for Google, Apple, GitHub and Microsoft, side by side or stacked.

props.name: layout
props.description: horizontal = one row, vertical = stacked full-width buttons

props.name: prefix
props.description: "Continue with" / "Sign in with" prefix; pass "" for icon + name only.

parts.name: SocialSignInButtons
parts.description: A grid with a 12 px gap: horizontal is one column below 640 px window width and one row of equal columns above, vertical is always one column. It has no border, background or role.

parts.name: Button
parts.description: One plain, rounded large Button per provider, as wide as its column. The label is the prefix plus the provider name on one line, or the name alone when the prefix is empty.

parts.name: Mark
parts.description: The provider's 16 px logo before the label, hidden from screen readers. Google and Microsoft keep their brand colours, Apple and GitHub take the text colour.

items.text: Use it where a person picks an account at Google, Apple, GitHub or Microsoft on a sign-in or sign-up screen. The sign-in itself is yours, the component only reports the choice.
Give each button room for its label: about 200 px with the prefix (two per row from 430 px) or 105 to 120 px without (four from 520 px). Otherwise go vertical.
Put a Divider with Label saying or between the buttons and an email form, and use the same prefix on every button of a screen: Sign up with, Continue with or Sign in with.
Show the wait and the failure next to the buttons. Wrap them in a disabled fieldset while a provider is pending, and write what happened, like Google sign-in was cancelled, not Something went wrong.
Offer only providers that work on the screen, since a button that leads nowhere is worse than a missing one. Keep the order the same on every screen.
Don't put three or four providers with a prefix in one row. The label does not wrap or shorten, it runs out of the button over the next one.
Don't draw your own marks or recolour the buttons. The marks follow each provider's brand guidelines, so use the component as it is.
Don't use the buttons to show which accounts are already connected, because they have no selected, connected or loading state. For connections use a list of rows with a button each.

components.title: Password Requirement
components.description: One password rule in a checklist that turns green once the password meets it.

parts.name: PasswordRequirement
parts.description: An li in a 12 px flex row with 8 px between icon and label, carrying a met data attribute when the rule is met. It renders no list, so put it inside a ul or ol.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: A 16 px Lucide icon: a check in a circle in the success colour when the rule is met, an empty circle when it is not. It is hidden from assistive technology.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The rule text, in the secondary colour when met and the tertiary colour when not. Add a visually hidden word for the state, such as met, so a screen reader reads it.

items.text: Put the requirements in a ul with an aria-label such as Password requirements. The component is an li, and a list tells a screen reader how many rules there are.
Add a hidden word after the label for the state, such as met or not met, in a screen-reader-only span. Without it the state is shown by icon and colour only, which a screen reader does not read.
Run every rule on each change and pass the result as met. Keep the rules in one array, so the list and the check that enables the submit button never disagree.
Say the total in a status line next to the list, such as 3 of 4 requirements met. It changes only when the count does, so a screen reader announces progress without reading the list on every key.
Point the password field at the list with aria-describedby, so the rules are read when the field gets focus.
Don't rely on the green icon alone to show a result, since people who cannot see colour miss it and the unmet circle is not an error. Keep the text and the hidden state word.
Don't show an unmet rule as an error before the person has typed. An empty field with every circle empty is the starting point, not a failure.
Don't use it for a checklist of tasks: it is a rule that a value passes or fails. Use Checklist Task for steps someone completes.

components.title: Password Strength
components.description: A four-step meter with a label that shows how strong a password is.

parts.name: PasswordStrength
parts.description: A column with 6 px between the segments and the label, announced politely. It fills the width of its parent, holds no state and tests nothing: you pass the level.

parts.name: Segments
parts.description: A row of four bars, 4 px high with 4 px between them, sharing the width equally. They carry no text and no role: they are drawn, not read.

parts.name: Segment
parts.description: One bar: the first one to four are filled with the colour of the level and the rest use the border colour. Weak fills 1, fair 2, good 3, strong 4.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The text under the bars in 12 px type, in the colour of the level: Weak password, Fair password, Good password or Strong password, or your own label. It is always shown.

items.text: Get the level from get password strength and render the meter only when it returns one (null for an empty password). Keep it mounted while the person types, so level changes are announced.
Leave the label on: it says the level in words, so colour is never the only signal, and a screen reader reads the label, not the bars. Pass your own label for other wording or another language.
Reserve the height of the meter and put a hint in it until the first key, as in the sign-up example, so the form does not jump when the meter appears.
Put the meter in a column as wide as the field above it. It fills the width of its parent.
Don't treat the helper as your password policy: it scores only length and character kinds, so Password1! scores strong. Enforce your real rules on the server and show them with Password Requirement.
Don't show a level for a password that is not typed. An empty field has no strength, and a weak bar for an empty field reads as an error.
Don't use real passwords in examples, tests or screenshots; use obviously made-up strings such as correct-horse. The demos keep them in local state and send nothing.

components.title: Backup Code
components.description: A recovery code that copies itself when clicked and is crossed out once it has been used.

parts.name: BackupCode
parts.description: A button with an 8 px radius, a 1 px border and the card fill. It is the only element: pressing it copies the code, and a used code is disabled.

parts.name: Code
parts.description: The code in 14 px medium text with tabular figures, on one line that wraps at a hyphen when the button is too narrow. A used code is struck through and tertiary.

parts.name: Copy icon
parts.description: A 14 px copy icon after the code. It is transparent until hover so it never shifts the code, and it is decorative because the code names the button.

items.text: Use Backup Code to list recovery codes after two-factor setup, in a grid with one code per button. For a single long value with a copy action, such as an invite URL, use Invite Link Row.
Mark codes that were already redeemed as used, so the list shows which ones are left. Say how many are left in text next to the grid, because the strike-through is visual only.
Confirm the copy in the copy handler, for example with a status line or a toast. It runs only after the clipboard took the code.
Offer a second way next to the list, such as Download as a text file, for the moment the clipboard is blocked.
Give each code a cell of at least 9 rem. A narrower box wraps the code at its hyphen.
Don't show your own Copied message on press. When the clipboard is blocked (an iframe, an http page, a denied permission) the copy handler does not run, and a message of your own would be wrong.
Don't rely on the copy icon to find the button. It shows on hover only, so on a touch screen the code itself is the target.
Don't use real codes in docs or tests. The demos here are made up and are not held anywhere.

components.title: Invite Row
components.description: An email field and a role picker for inviting one person, with a button to remove the row.

props.name: stacked
props.description: Stack email over role on small screens (Figma Type=email role stacked).

parts.name: InviteRow
parts.description: A flex container with a 12 px gap between the email and the role, with no border or fill. From the small breakpoint up they sit in one row; below that, or when stacked, one over the other.

parts.name: Email field
parts.description: An Input of type email, named Email, that takes the rest of the row. It shows the placeholder info@wunderui.com while empty.

parts.name: Role select
parts.description: A NativeSelect named Role, at least 9 rem wide, with the roles you pass. The list opens below the field.

parts.name: Remove button
parts.description: A plain icon button with a 16 px X, named Remove. It is drawn only when you pass a remove handler.

items.text: Use Invite Row for each person in a team invite list, one row per invitee. For one shareable link, use Invite Link Row.
Keep it controlled: pass the email and role with their change handlers. Without the handlers the fields don't change when someone types or picks.
Pass your own roles when the defaults (Admin, Editor, Viewer) don't match the product, and make sure the current role is one of them.
Use the stacked layout in a narrow container. The row switches layout with the screen width, not its container's, so a narrow dialog on a wide screen stays inline.
Validate in your handler and write the message under the row, like Enter a valid email address. The row has no error state, so name the address when checking several rows.
After a row is removed, move focus to the list and say which address went in a status line. Every remove button is named just Remove.
Don't pass a remove handler to a row you must keep. The remove button is drawn only when the handler exists.
Don't use real addresses in docs or tests. The addresses in the demos belong to made-up people.

components.title: Settings Row
components.description: A setting's title and description with a switch, or any other control, on the right.

props.name: control
props.description: Trailing control: a Button, Switch, Badge … Pass `switch` props instead for the toggle variant.

parts.name: SettingsRow
parts.description: A flex row with the text on the left, the control on the right and 24 px between them, centred vertically. It has no padding, border or fill, because the list around it provides them.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The title in 14 px medium text, wrapped when long with no ellipsis. With a switch it is the name of the switch.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: The description in 12 px secondary text, 2 px under the title. Drawn only when passed.

parts.name: Control
parts.description: A switch when a checked value or change handler is set, otherwise the control you pass, such as a button, select or badge. It keeps its size and is never squeezed.

items.text: Use it for lists of preferences, one setting per row. For choices between described options use Selector Item.
Pass the checked value and a change handler for a switch. The title names the switch for assistive technology.
Pass your own control for a setting that opens something or shows a state: a Button, a Select, a Badge. Give a Switch passed this way its own aria-label, because the title cannot name it.
Pass your own Switch as the control when it must show that it is saving or disabled. The built-in switch supports neither.
Space rows with the list: a divider between rows with vertical padding on each gives one hairline between two rows, never two. Put the list in a card with a 16 px radius.
Say what changed in a status line, such as Email notifications turned off, because a switch that flips alone gives a screen reader user no other news.
Don't pass both a switch and a control. When the checked value or change handler is set, the control is ignored.
Don't put a destructive action behind a plain press. A destructive button should open a confirmation, and the result should be undoable when possible.
Don't expect the description to be announced with the switch. It is not linked to the control, so keep what matters in the title.

components.title: Agenda Event
components.description: One event in an agenda list, with its start and end time, a color bar, details and guests.

props.name: wrap
props.description: The title and the meta line wrap onto more lines instead of clamping (title, 2 lines) and truncating (meta). Default: false.

parts.name: AgendaEvent
parts.description: One schedule row with a line below it. With a click handler the title becomes a button stretched over the whole row, with a hover fill and a focus ring.

parts.name: Time
parts.description: The start time above an optional end time, in a fixed 64 px column, printed as written.

parts.name: Colour bar
parts.description: A 3 px bar in the event colour (one of eight, purple by default). It is always shown.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The title, up to two lines, then an ellipsis. With a click handler it is a native button named by the title.

parts.name: Details
parts.description: A line under the title in smaller tertiary text, such as the room or call link. Cut to one line.

parts.name: Guests
parts.description: Overlapping avatars: the first three, then a +N count for the rest.

parts.name: Menu button
parts.description: A small icon button named Event menu, shown when a menu handler is set. It sits above the stretched title, so clicking it does not open the event.

parts.name: AgendaEventChip
parts.description: The compact form of an event for a day cell of a month grid: a 24 px label with a 3 px coloured bar and the truncated title. It is a button, so a Popover or Menu trigger can render it. It replaces EventChip.

items.text: Use an Agenda Event for a schedule row with guests, a menu or a detail view to open. For a plain read-only list of times and titles, use Agenda.
Pass a click handler instead of wrapping the row in a link or button. The title becomes a real button over the whole row, and the menu button stays reachable.
Keep the title short and put the place or call details on the line below it.
Give every guest a name. It becomes the avatar's hover title and the source of the initials when there is no photo.
Put rows in a bordered, rounded container with the last line removed and the outer corners rounded. Each row draws its own line below, so the last one would double the border.
Don't let the colour bar carry the meaning alone. It has no text, so name the kind of event in the title or detail line too.
Don't add overflow-hidden to the container. It clips the focus ring, which is drawn outside the row.
Don't put buttons or links inside the title or detail line. The title is already a button, and a control inside a button is invalid HTML; use the menu for extra actions.
Pass wrap where the meta line or the title runs long (phones): nothing is clamped or truncated.

components.title: Form Actions
components.description: The row of buttons at the end of a form, aligned right, left or spread to both edges.

parts.name: FormActions
parts.description: The row. It lays its children out 8 px apart and wraps them onto a second line on a narrow screen; align sets where it sits: end (default), start or between.

parts.name: Secondary action
parts.description: The way out of the form: Cancel, Discard or Back. A plain Button that doesn't compete with the main action, and it is disabled while the main action is pending.

parts.name: Main action
parts.description: The gradient Button that submits the form, one per row. It shows pending, success or error, with a label that says what is happening.

parts.name: Destructive action
parts.description: An action that loses something, such as Delete draft. It sits at the other edge so a quick tap on the main action can't land on it; an irreversible step still needs its own confirmation.

items.text: Use Form Actions for the buttons that end a form, dialog, sheet or step. Buttons that act on the page, not the form, belong in a Toolbar.
Put the main action last, next to the way out: Cancel, then Save changes. Write both as verbs that say what happens: Create project, not OK.
Keep the DOM order equal to the screen order, so Tab follows what the eye sees. The main action comes last at the end, first when aligned to the start.
While saving, show a pending main action with its own label (Saving…) and disable the way out. Afterwards show Saved for a moment.
Put a destructive action at the opposite edge and group the other two together. Ask in an Alert Dialog before an irreversible delete.
Match the size of the fields above the row (32, 36 or 40 px) and use one size for every button in it.
Don't put two gradient buttons in a row. One main action per row; the second is a plain Button.
Don't hide the main action under a menu, and don't disable it without saying why. If there is nothing to save, say so in a status line.
Don't reorder the buttons with CSS to move the main action. Tab order stays the same and stops matching the screen.

hooks.name: useDensity
hooks.summary: Reads and changes the density of the nearest DensityProvider.
hooks.description: Density sets the size of controls, fields and rows: `compact` (the default, controls 32–48 px) or `comfortable` (36–56 px). `useDensity` returns the density the nearest `DensityProvider` applies and a setter for it, so a settings page can offer the switch.

properties.name: density
properties.description: `"compact"` or `"comfortable"`: the density the provider applies to the document.

properties.name: setDensity
properties.description: Changes the density for the whole document. When the provider persists, the choice is written to localStorage as well. Calling it with the current value does nothing visible.

notes: Outside a `DensityProvider` it returns `compact` and a setter that does nothing.
The provider sets `data-density` on `<html>`, so portals such as menus and dialogs follow it. For one region only, wrap it in `<Density value>` instead.
With a `storageKey` on the provider the choice is kept in localStorage. Add `densityScript()` to the document head, so a stored `comfortable` paints before the first frame.
Switching density changes the layout without animation: the provider pauses transitions for one frame.

examples.title: A density setting
examples.description: A settings row that switches the whole document. The form below it reads the same tokens as every other control.

examples.title: Keep the choice without a flash
examples.description: The provider stores the choice. `densityScript()` applies it in the document head, before the first paint.

examples.title: Control the density yourself
examples.description: Pass `density` and `onDensityChange` to keep the value in your own state, a user profile or the URL. The hook then reports and requests changes.

hooks.name: useIcon
hooks.summary: The component for a built-in icon name: the one of the nearest `IconProvider`, otherwise the Lucide default.

hooks.name: useScrollSpy
hooks.summary: Tells which section of a page or a scroll container is being read.
hooks.description: Pass the ids of the section headings. The hook returns the id of the last section whose top has passed the reading line, a quarter down the window or the container, and a setter to move the marker yourself. At the end of the scroll the last section wins, so a short closing section still becomes active.
hooks.signature: useScrollSpy(ids: string[], root?: React.RefObject<HTMLElement | null> | undefined, enabled?: boolean): readonly [string | undefined, React.Dispatch<React.SetStateAction<string | undefined>>]

params.name: ids
params.description: The ids of the section elements, in the order they appear on the page. An id without an element in the page is ignored.

params.name: root
params.description: A ref to the element that scrolls the sections. Leave it out when the page itself scrolls. The sections are looked up inside this element, and the reading line is a quarter of its height from its top.

params.name: enabled
params.description: Set it to `false` to stop listening, for example while the list is hidden. The marker keeps its last value.

properties.name: active
properties.description: The id of the section being read. Before the first measurement it is the first id.

properties.name: setActive
properties.description: Moves the marker yourself, usually in the click handler of a list item. The next scroll measures again and takes over.

notes: `FloatingToc` uses it when you leave out `activeId`; reach for the hook when you build your own navigation.
Pass a ref as `root` when the sections scroll inside a container instead of the window.
`enabled={false}` stops listening, for example while a drawer that holds the list is closed.
Call the setter on click so the marker moves at once, before the smooth scroll arrives.

examples.title: Inside a scroll container
examples.description: A settings panel that scrolls on its own. `root` points at the panel, so the sections are looked up inside it and the reading line is a quarter of its height.

examples.title: Track the page
examples.description: Without `root` the hook watches the window, for a long article with a table of contents beside it.

examples.title: Pause while the list is hidden
examples.description: A drawer holds the section list. While it is closed nobody sees the marker, so the hook stops listening.

hooks.name: useToast
hooks.summary: Shows, updates and closes toasts from anywhere below a Toaster.
hooks.description: Returns the toast manager of the nearest `Toaster`. Call `add` with a title, an optional description and a type, and the toast slides into the corner the Toaster was given. `add` returns the toast's id, which `update` and `close` take.

properties.name: toasts
properties.description: The toasts that are open right now, newest first. The component re-renders whenever the list changes.

properties.name: add
properties.description: Shows a toast and returns its id. Options: `title`, `description`, `type` (`success`, `error`, `warning`, `info`), `timeout` in ms (`0` keeps it open), `priority` (`low` or `high`), `actionProps` for an inline action such as Undo, `onClose`, `onRemove` and `id`. Adding with an id that is already open updates that toast and restarts its timer.

properties.name: close
properties.description: Closes the toast with that id. Without an id it closes every open toast.

properties.name: update
properties.type: <T extends Data = Data>(toastId: string, options: ToastManagerUpdateOptions<T> | ((prevToast: ToastObject<T>) => ToastManagerUpdateOptions<T>)) => void
properties.description: Changes an open toast in place: pass the fields to change, or a function that gets the previous toast and returns them. The toast keeps its place in the stack.

properties.name: promise
properties.type: <Value, T extends Data = Data>(promise: Promise<Value>, options: ToastManagerPromiseOptions<Value, T>) => Promise<Value>
properties.description: Shows the `loading` toast, then turns it into `success` or `error` when the promise settles. Each state is a title string or the same options as `add`; `success` and `error` can be functions of the result. Returns the promise, so you can await it.

notes: Mount `Toaster` once, high in the tree (the root layout). Without it, `add` has nowhere to render.
`type` sets the colour of the dot: `success`, `error`, `warning` or `info` (the default).
Toasts close after 5 seconds. Pass `timeout` to keep one longer, or `0` to keep it until it is closed.
Use a toast to confirm something that already happened. A decision the user still has to make belongs in a Dialog.

examples.title: Confirm an action
examples.description: A form that saves and tells the person it worked. The toast confirms what already happened.

examples.title: Follow a request
examples.description: `promise` shows a loading toast and turns it into the result, so one call covers all three states.

examples.title: Update a toast in place
examples.description: `add` returns the id of the toast. A `timeout` of `0` keeps it open while the work runs; `update` then turns it into the result.

durations.use: Tooltip dismiss, press release. Barely reads as motion.
The default exit. Hover, focus ring, checkbox, switch track.
Dropdown, popover, context menu, backdrop, collapse.
Dialog, toast, switch thumb — a surface arriving.
A side panel and a full-width panel. Rare.
Progress and meter fills. Data moving, not chrome.

easings.use: Anything arriving. Fast start, long settle. The house curve.
Anything repositioning while staying on screen.
Dialog, popover, switch. At most one per screen.
A sampled spring: one soft overshoot, then it settles. Something physical landing — a thumb, an arrow, a released sheet. Never on a data value.

amplitudes.use: Tooltip — stays glued to its anchor.

rules: **Duration and easing are class names, not numbers.** `duration-base`, `ease-entrance`. Tailwind has no `--duration-*` theme namespace, so WunderUI ships these as `@utility` rules that also set `--tw-duration` — which means they work on `animate-in` / `animate-out` too.
**Only `transform` and `opacity`.** Everything else goes through layout or paint. Height animates via `grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr`, never via `height`.
**Entrances decelerate, exits accelerate.** `ease-entrance` in, `ease-exit` out — and the exit is one step shorter on the duration scale, never the entrance duration reversed.
**Never fade in the LCP element.** An element at `opacity: 0` is not an LCP candidate, so a 600ms hero fade adds 600ms to your LCP. Render headline copy at full opacity; animate `transform` only.
**Restrain the travel.** Anything anchored to a trigger moves `--travel-xs` or `--travel-sm`. A menu that slides 20px looks like it fell in.

**One overshoot per screen.** `ease-overshoot` is punctuation. Two of them on one view and the interface reads as a toy. Never on a data value: a bar, gauge or bubble that swings past its number shows a wrong number for a moment.

**Reduced motion is opt-in, not a kill switch.** Wrap the animation in `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)` so the still state is the default and you cannot forget a selector. Reduced means calmer, not nothing: drop transforms and travel, keep opacity and colour changes (rule 15).

**Never `transition-all`.** Name the properties — `transition-[opacity,transform]` — or use bare `transition`, which covers colour, shadow, transform and opacity but no layout property. `transition-all` animates things you did not mean to animate, including on first paint.
**Loading keeps its height.** A skeleton occupies the same box as the content it stands in for, and crossfades — it never collapses and reflows.
**A looping ambient animation is the one place `ease-in-out` belongs.** A shimmer that runs forever has no entrance and no exit, so symmetry is correct there and nowhere else.

**Animate by frequency.** Keyboard-driven and 100+/day actions (command palette, shortcuts, moving between tooltips) get no motion; tens a day get a short fade; rare moments may delight. Tooltips skip their entrance when another one was just open (`data-open:data-instant:animate-none`).

**Anchored surfaces grow from their trigger.** Popover, dropdown, tooltip, hover card and select use `origin-(--transform-origin)`. Never start from `scale(0)` — start at 0.92–0.97 with opacity. Centred dialogs are exempt.

**Toggles stay interruptible.** Animate switches, checkboxes, tabs and other repeated state changes with transitions — they retarget from wherever they are — never with keyframes bound to the state, which restart from zero. An overshoot transition (`transition-transform duration-base ease-overshoot`) still swings past the end.

**Hover only where hover exists.** Tailwind v4's `hover:` is already gated to `(hover: hover)`; hand-written `:hover` in CSS goes inside `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)`, so a tap on a phone does not leave a hover state stuck.

**Reduced motion keeps the fade.** WunderUI's global rule zeroes the scale, slide, spin and blur of every `animate-in` / `animate-out` and every transform transition, and keeps opacity and colour — so do not add `motion-reduce:transition-none` or `motion-reduce:animate-none` to a fade.

recipes.Overlay enter and exit:
/* Dialog, sheet, popover, dropdown, context menu — one pattern for all of them.
   Base UI exposes data-open / data-closed; tw-animate-css turns them into keyframes. */
<Dialog.Popup className="
  data-open:animate-in   data-open:fade-in-0   data-open:zoom-in-92
  data-open:slide-in-from-bottom-2
  data-open:duration-slow  data-open:ease-overshoot
  data-closed:animate-out  data-closed:fade-out-0 data-closed:zoom-out-96
  data-closed:duration-fast data-closed:ease-exit
" />

topics.summary: Install the package or add the source, wire up the styles and the @source path.

topics.title: Rules for agents
topics.summary: The rules every screen follows: tokens, theming, imports, composites, motion.
topics.body:
1. **Never hardcode colours.** Every value is a CSS variable. Use the Tailwind utility that maps to it (`bg-card`, `text-text-secondary`, `border-border`), not a hex.
2. **Theme by overriding tokens**, not by restyling components. Setting `--primary` on any wrapper re-themes everything inside it.
3. **Dark mode is a `.dark` class on `<html>`.** `ThemeProvider` (next-themes) handles it. Never write your own dark colours.
4. **The package is client code.** It ships with a `"use client"` banner, so you can import it inside React Server Components, but its own components run on the client.
5. **Import from the package root**, never from `dist/` or `src/` paths.
6. `cn` is not re-exported — import it from the `cn` package directly.
7. **Prefer a composite over rebuilding one.** Before writing a table, a board, a stat row or a chat bubble by hand, check the task table and the inventory below — it probably exists.
8. **Charts take a `loading` prop**; do not build your own skeleton.
10. **Motion comes from tokens too.** Duration is `duration-instant|fast|base|slow|deliberate|ambient`, easing is `ease-entrance|exit|move|overshoot|spring`. Never write a raw `duration-300` and never write `ease-in-out` — both are the default every generator reaches for, and both read as mechanical.
11. **A chart enters in 1.1 s, in a dashboard in 0.8 s.** The duration is the `--chart-enter` token; the dashboard load sequence shortens it by itself, any other dense screen sets `data-chart-motion="dense"` on a wrapper. Never give a chart its own duration, and never replay the entrance to show new data — Area, Line and Bar charts morph to it.
13. **Two series are indigo and pink.** Leave `color` off and the series take the standard order (indigo, pink, blue, green, orange, purple, yellow, grey). Red is not in it: set it by name, and only for a negative value or a limit that was passed.

topics.title: Task → component
topics.summary: Which component to use for a task — look here before building anything by hand.
topics.body:
Look here first. Most requests map to something that already exists.

| I need … | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Plain table markup, no behaviour | `Table` and its parts |
| Editable cells inside a table | `CellSelect`, `CellSwitch`, `CellSlider`, `CellColorPicker` |
| Formatted table cells | `UserCell`, `BadgeCell`, `CurrencyCell`, `ProgressCell`, `TagCell`, `RatingCell` |
| Bulk actions for a selection | `ActionBar` |
| A percentage change as a small pill | `TrendChip` |
| Modal for a focused task | `Dialog` |
| Confirmation with consequences | `AlertDialog` |
| Text input that suggests while typing | `Combobox` or `Autocomplete` |
| Pick a date | `DatePicker`, or `Calendar` for an inline month |
| Form with labels and validation | `Form` + `Field` + `Fieldset` |
| Settings row with a toggle | `SelectorItem` + `Switch`, grouped in `SelectorItemGroup` |
| Switch between views, compactly | `Segment`; `Tabs` when the views are panels |
| File upload | `DropZone` |
| Nothing to show yet | `EmptyState` |
| Something is loading | `Skeleton`; charts take `loading` |
| Transient notification | `useToast` with `Toaster`; `Alert` when it should stay |
| Chronological events | `Timeline`; `Agenda` for scheduled ones |
| Folder and file tree | `FileTree` |
| Time an interaction | `duration-fast` hover/press and every exit · `duration-base` menus · `duration-slow` dialogs · `duration-deliberate` sheets · `duration-ambient` data bars |
| Ease an interaction | `ease-entrance` arriving · `ease-exit` leaving · `ease-move` repositioning · `ease-overshoot` once per screen at most |
| Animate something open or closed | `data-open` / `data-closed` variants; height via `grid-rows-[0fr]` → `[1fr]` |
